#303. €561 Billion and Still Not Enough: Germany's 2027 Budget Exposes a Coalition on the Brink

The budget for 2027 has reached new highs, and pension funds, defense spending and a weak economy are increasing the pressure. At the same time, tensions are mounting within the government.

At first glance, everything seems to be business as usual. Lawmakers in the Bundestag, the lower house of parliament, are holding four days of final debates on how much money the federal government may spend in the coming year, and on what. These follow a familiar pattern: The government pats itself on the back, while the opposition voices criticism. But anyone listening more closely will notice that there are doubts even in the ranks of the coalition parties, the conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU), their Bavarian allies, the Christian Social Union (CSU), and the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD).

"As a country, we are in a difficult situation geopolitically, technologically, and demographically, and next year's budget is an accurate reflection of that," Chancellor Friedrich Merz (CDU) acknowledged on Wednesday in the Bundestag.

"If we don't change course, in a few years we'll find ourselves in a situation where all federal revenue will have to be spent on social programs, interest payments, and defense," he reflected on Wednesday during a four-hour debate focused on government policy as a whole, rather than the individual budgets of the ministries.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

This government has now been in office for about 20 months. Back in early 2025, expectations were enormous. Merz had promised to bring the budget back in line with the debt brake enshrined in the constitution, which stipulates that the government can spend only slightly more than it collects (with exceptions now made for defense and security).

Yet for 2027, spending — at just under €561 billion ($614 billion) — will be higher than ever before, and tax revenues are nowhere near sufficient to cover this, meaning Germany is looking at record borrowing for the year totaling €210 billion.

The largest opposition party, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) calculated that the government will incur €401,000 in new debt every minute next year. In the Bundestag, AfD co-leader Tino Chrupalla called it a "debt orgy" that will paralyze the country. Merz will "go down in history as the chancellor who led Germany to bankruptcy," he exclaimed.

Germany's budget deficit has only ever been higher in the COVID-19 pandemic. The current pressures are obvious: The economy is struggling, the population aging, and Russia's war against Ukraine is about to enter its sixth year.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The defense budget is now by far the highest in the history of the Federal Republic, with €109 billion allocated for 2027, an increase of €27 billion on last year. Added to this is the multi-year, debt-financed special military fund, intended to modernize the armed forces, bringing the total defense budget to €139 billion.

The AfD and the socialist Left Party have sharply criticized this. Left Party parliamentary leader Heidi Reichinnek accused the government of pursuing "militarization and boundless rearmament on the one hand, and brutal social cuts and an orgy of budget cuts on the other."

The AfD's Chrupalla said that the temporary reduction in the electricity tax, pushed through at the last minute, would save the average family a mere €100 a year, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy "walks out of the chancellery here in Berlin with a check for €200 million after just one afternoon."

"Whose chancellor are you, Mr. Merz?" he asked.

The opposition Greens did not agree. While they also criticized the budget as "unserious," Green Party Bundestag member Britta Haßelmann described the AfD's stance on Ukraine as shameful. She rejected the idea that money was being wasted on Ukraine, saying that supporting Ukraine bolstered security for Germany and Europe.

The chancellor shares this view. "You can't say it often enough, either to the far right or the far left: Russia knows exactly what it wants. And Russia wants more than just Ukraine," Merz said.

He added that Russia is escalating tensions in the Baltic region, in Poland, in the Black Sea, and in space; and that Moscow is also seeking escalation in Germany, even at the cost of lives. "That is why we must show Russia its limits," he said.

But it is becoming increasingly difficult for the government to justify the high spending on Ukraine. Germany's pension and health care costs are only getting bigger: By far the largest single budget item is that of the Ministry of Labor and Social Affairs, which is rising to over €200 billion, even with cuts to unemployment benefits.

Work is currently underway on a reform of the pension system — something that many see as urgent, as the workforce born in the 1960s, when more than a million children were born in Germany every year, is on brink of retiring. Birth rates nearly halved by the mid-1970s and declined even further afterward. For now, so-called "boomers" still make up one-third of the current workforce — but soon they will be drawing pensions.

Even now, Germany's pensions cannot be financed solely with contributions on wages and salaries. In 2025, just over €420 billion in pensions were paid out, with the government contributing €127 billion of that amount. By 2027, the government aims to save €3 billion on this figure, which is likely to further increase pension contributions.

The coalition parties are stuck in a row over how to reform the pension system. Chancellor Merz insisted in the Bundestag that the coalition was solving the country's fundamental problems, but he warned that in future, tax revenues "will no longer be enough to afford everything we have become all too accustomed to," he said. "All of us here will have to give up some of the ideas we cherish."

The SPD, on the other hand, is counting on increasing federal revenue. Its parliamentary leader Matthias Miersch emphasized in the Bundestag that large fortunes and inheritances must contribute more to "public costs."

That, he said, must also apply to large companies. Currently, heirs to family-owned businesses often pay significantly less in taxes than heirs to real estate or financial assets, because they can be exempted from inheritance tax if they continue to run the business. This is intended to protect them from having to pay taxes in the event of a breakup or sale of the company.

According to Miersch, the government must now think about taxing the wealthy more. "For us, this issue is by no means off the table; on the contrary, we are putting it on the agenda," he said. The government's revenue situation is "an issue we need to discuss."

All in all, the outlook for 2027 is strained — and not just financially. The political differences between the CDU/CSU and the SPD are likely to make working together even more difficult. Conflict is inevitable, especially with several state elections scheduled for the spring.

The chancellor knows this and tried to appear confident that better collaboration was possible. "We must seek compromise in our joint decision-making, represented by these — admittedly quite different — coalition partners," he said.

This article was originally written in German.

#302. Giving Marjorie Taylor Greene a platform isn't good for America

Editor’s Note:  Dean Obeidallah, a former attorney, is the host of SiriusXM radio’s daily program “The Dean Obeidallah Show.” Follow him @DeanObeidallah@masto.ai. The opinions expressed in this commentary are his own. View more opinion on CNN.

Last year, GOP Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia spoke at a white nationalist event organized by Holocaust denier Nick Fuentes that caused Republican leaders to denounce her.

Last week, Greene’s Twitter account was temporarily suspended by the Elon Musk-headed platform over a tweet with a graphic referring to a “Trans Day of Vengeance,” as she denounced a planned transgender rights rally.

And come Tuesday, Greene has announced plans to protest in New York City when former President Donald Trump is expected to be arraigned on an indictment of more than 30 counts, calling the proceedings against him an “unconstitutional WITCH HUNT!”

But on Sunday, Greene was featured on CBS’ “60 Minutes” in an interview the long-running show promoted on Twitter with the tease: “Republican Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene, nicknamed MTG, isn’t afraid to share her opinions, no matter how intense and in-your-face they are. She sits down with Lesley Stahl this Sunday on 60 Minutes.” The images attached to this tweet by “60 Minutes” include Greene and Stahl walking through the US Capitol, taking a stroll outside and Greene showing Stahl something on her phone.

It's time for Marjorie Taylor Greene to go

In the segment that aired Sunday night, Stahl noted the congresswoman had moved from the fringe to the GOP’s front row in two years despite a “sharp tongue” and “some pretty radical views” as well as “over the top” comments such as “the Democrats are a party of pedophiles.” Stahl also referred to video of Greene chasing a Parkland, Florida, school shooting survivor, still maintaining that the 2020 election was stolen and failing to criticize Trump over spending. (The interview was conducted before news of his indictment.)

But Stahl didn’t mention Greene spoke at a white nationalist event a year ago while a member of Congress or her extreme anti-Muslim views and her defense of January 6 rioters.

Criticism of CBS for amplifying Greene has been swift and well-deserved even before the program aired. Former GOP Rep. Adam Kinzinger of Illinois tweeted beforehand: “Wow. Insane that 60 min would do this.” (Kinzinger is a CNN senior political commentator.)

Journalist Molly Jong-Fast also slammed “60 Minutes” with the tweet: “Attention is currency and 60 minutes is spending its currency on the Jewish space lasers woman.” (Jong-Fast was apparently referring to Greene’s past claim that a massive California wildfire was started by “a laser” beamed from space controlled by a prominent Jewish banking family.)

David Hogg, who survived the 2018 horrific school shooting at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland and has since become an activist against gun violence, responded, “I look forward to your questions about why she thinks school shootings are fake and why she’s supported QAnon.”

Greene amplified the conspiracy theory — two years before being elected to Congress — that the Parkland shooting that took 17 lives was staged. And in 2019, Greene appeared on video confronting Hogg outside the Capitol when he was championing laws to save lives from gun violence, screaming that the then-teenager was a “coward.” She also called Hogg “#littleHitler” on social media.

Greene’s own tweet promoting Sunday’s segment was not filled with her typical smears of “fake news” when she doesn’t like the coverage. Rather, Greene urged people to tune in as she praised “60 Minutes” host Stahl (and misspelled her first name): “It was an honor to spend a few days with the legendary icon Leslie Stahl and talented crew @60Minutes.” Greene added, “Leslie is a trailblazer for women in journalism. And while we may disagree on some issues, I respect her greatly.”

Now, it is true that “60 Minutes” over its 50-plus-year history has featured what the show has dubbed “controversial” guests. These include a 2000 interview with Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh, whose 1995 terrorist attack left 168 dead, including 19 children. And the show did a 1979 interview with Iran’s Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini.

Perhaps “60 Minutes” views Greene — who has repeatedly downplayed and even defended the January 6, 2021, attack plus called for the GOP to become the party of “Christian nationalism” — in the vein of its long list of controversial guests. (CBS had not responded to a request from CNN for comment at time of publishing.)

However, the choice of Greene as a guest instantly recalls the comments of then-CBS CEO Les Moonves during Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign when he admitted that Trump’s candidacy “may not be good for America, but it’s damn good for CBS.” Moonves added, “The money’s rolling in and this is fun. … (T)his is going to be a very good year for us,” concluding, “Sorry. It’s a terrible thing to say. But bring it on, Donald. Keep going.”

Moonves may be gone from CBS, but it appears his mindset continues at “60 Minutes.” And that may be good for “60 Minutes,” but it’s definitely not good for America.

#301. Molly Ringwald, Yellowjackets, and a major change for Van

You might have clocked it in the Season 4 premiere, but with episode 2 it's very clear: Molly Ringwald has joined Yellowjackets.

The '80s icon who fronted movies like The Breakfast Club, Sixteen Candles, and Pretty in Pink takes over the role of Van's (Liv Hewson) mom, Vicky Palmer, from Deborah Vancelette. And this signifies a major change in Van's life, post-rescue.

In the Season 1 pilot, Vicky (Vancelette) is presented as a bad mom. In a montage of the Yellowjackets readying for that fateful flight, Van walks through a dark, cluttered house to find her mom passed out on the couch, next to a nearly empty alcohol bottle. She tries to wake her, presumably because she needs a ride to the plane. But calling to her and shaking her isn't enough to rouse Vicky. So, Van slaps her, and she does so with a world-weariness that suggests this isn't an isolated incident.

In Season 4, episode 2, Vicky (Ringwald) is transformed. The living room is sunny and tidy upon Van's return, with a wall of VHS tapes carefully preserved. Later, Vicky shows she cares by assuring Van she taped every episode of The X-Files. To Tai (Jasmin Savoy Brown), she'll say of Vicky, "My mom is completely different."

No shade to Vancelette, who got little to do in the role of Vicky. But if any Yellowjacket was going to get a mom played by a movie idol of the '80s, it ought to be Van. Her love of pop culture is a defining characteristic, as she'd quote and allude to movies and shows to brandish her wit and wisdom. Of course, if her mom's going to get a glow-up, she's going to become the "princess" from The Breakfast Club. #300. Best Black Friday Robot Vacuum Deals from Roborock (2026): Up to $700 Off

Robot vacuums are more expensive than ever, with models from popular brands starting anywhere from $1,200. Even Roborock's latest top-of-the-line vacuums are now pushing closer to $2,000 in starting price. But you usually don't have to pay such a high price tag for a great model—you just have to wait for a good sale, and Black Friday deals have arrived, with the best sales you'll find before the holidays.

Black Friday is easily one of the best times to buy a robot vacuum, and Roborock makes one of the biggest ranges of robot vacuums that we love. Roborock's vacuums all have great navigation, but they come with varying levels of mop style, suction power, and other features, depending on how much you want to spend. But you'll spend much less shopping Roborock's Black Friday deals happening right now.

The Roborock Qrevo 2 Pro launched in late summer as the newest addition to the brand's more affordable Qrevo line, and it quickly landed as a pick on my guide to the Best Robot Vacuums. It's often on sale for around $600, and thanks to Black Friday, it's down to the lowest price I've seen it for: $450, nearly half off.

Overall, Roborock's vacuums are great, but I've been especially impressed by this one's corner cleaning, thanks to its extendable mop arm. It won't always spot cords, but it does a better job at navigating furniture and getting underneath my cabinets than more expensive robot vacuums I've tested.

If you'd rather have a roller-mop-style robot vacuum, the Roborock Qrevo Curv 2 Flow is another great option from Roborock's Qrevo line. This one came out in January of this year, and our reviewer instantly loved it.

The Qrevo Curv 2 Flow is a more expensive robot vacuum than the Qrevo 2 since it comes with the brand's SpriaFlow roller-mop. The internal roller spans nearly the entire width of the vacuum and can extend to edge-clean your home. It even has a built-in scraper to move dirty water into the tank instead of rolling it back onto the floor. If you're looking for an affordable mopping powerhouse, this is the one to choose. It's also nearly half off, down to $550 off the $1,000 price tag.

There's the affordable Qrevo line from Roborock, and then there's the higher-end Saros line. While neither I nor former WIRED reviewer Adrienne So were particularly impressed with the Saros 20, I've been much happier with the performance of the Saros 20 Flow. Like the Curv 2 Flow, it has a roller mop instead of spinning mop pads, and it did well in my mopping tests. It also didn't leave debris around, even with its high suction of 36,000 Pa.

It's one of Roborock's most expensive vacuums, and it comes across while using it—it feels very premium. I've been preferring it over the new Dyson robot vacuum I've been testing. Luckily, you can get it on sale right now for Black Friday. It still isn't cheap at $1,300, but it's one of my all-time favorites and one I have kept coming back to after trying other models.

If you're looking for something truly unique in a robot vacuum, Roborock's Saros Z70 might be what you're looking for. It has a mechanical arm built into it to pick up small items like socks while it vacuums, which sounds handy, but it didn't work as well as we'd hoped during testing. Still, maybe you feel that's the solution you've been dying for. If that's the case, it's available for a nice discount right now at $950.

It also packs 22,000 Pa of suction (not as powerful as the Saros 20 Flow, but still plenty of suction to clean carpets and rugs alike!) and still executes fast, effective cleaning. But the battery life on this vacuum isn't as long as that of other Roborocks we've tested. Again, you're mostly getting this one for the mechanical arm.

#297. Macy's postpones Thanksgiving Day Parade due to severe weather

Macy's on Wednesday announced it's postponing its Thanksgiving Day Parade, originally scheduled for Thursday, due to severe weather.

The parade, held each year on Thanksgiving morning, will now take place on Saturday at 8:30 a.m. ET, according to the company. The New York City area is expected to have heavy rain and thunderstorms on Thanksgiving.

"The safety of our participants and spectators is our top priority, and after close consultation with our city and agency partners, we have made the decision to move this year's celebration," Macy's said in a statement.

This year's event marks the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade. The annual event has never been canceled due to weather, though it was suspended between 1942 and 1944 for World War II.

The parade's viability this year had been in question after concerns arose over strong winds that could become dangerous for the massive balloons that the event is known for. Many of the balloons had already been inflated as of Wednesday afternoon.

The postponement also means thousands of volunteers and artists slated to perform will have to adapt to Saturday's schedule.

#295. Peter Magyar meets Volodymyr Zelenskyy: Hungary and Ukraine make a fresh start after the icy relations of the Viktor Orban era

After years of frosty and hostile relations under Hungary's Kremlin-friendly former PM Viktor Orban, his successor, Peter Magyar, and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy seek to reset their countries' ties.

The location and the gesture were carefully chosen: Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stood side by side, laid flowers and bowed their heads at the military cemetery in the center of the Ukrainian city of Uzhhorod.

One of those buried there is an ethnic Hungarian who was one of the first soldiers killed in Russia's full-scale war of aggression against Ukraine.

Magyar intentionally chose not to begin his first visit to Ukraine as prime minister at a government building. Instead, his Tuesday afternoon visit began at a place where he could demonstrate his solidarity with Ukraine more clearly than anywhere else.

Uzhhorod, known as Ungvar in Hungarian, is the capital of Ukraine's Transcarpathia region, which is home to around 80,000 members of Ukraine's Hungarian minority. Thousands of ethnic Hungarians are fighting Russian occupying forces on the front lines.

For Hungary, where ethnic Hungarian minorities in neighboring countries traditionally play an important role, the war is therefore closer to home than it is for other European countries.

Magyar described his visit to Ukraine as a "historic day" in a Facebook post. Before the ceremony at the cemetery in Uzhhorod, he said: "I bring with me the solidarity of the Hungarian people. We stand with Ukraine against the Russian aggressor."

Zelenskyy responded on X, saying "We appreciate this gesture of respect toward those who sacrificed their lives for Ukraine's independence."

The meeting between Magyar and Zelenskyy marked a turning point in Hungary's approach to Ukraine.

The two leaders repeatedly shook hands throughout the day. Such scenes would have been unthinkable just a few months ago. The propaganda of Magyar's pro-Russian predecessor, Viktor Orban, portrayed Ukraine as a "mafia state" and "lawless country" on an almost daily basis.

Under Orban, relations between Hungary and Ukraine reached a historic low.

Now the two countries are seeking a political reset, which is important not only for Hungary and Ukraine but for Europe as a whole. After all, Orban's repeated obstruction of support for Ukraine drove the EU to the brink of despair.

During talks in Uzhhorod, the two leaders also agreed to closer economic cooperation.

The talks centered on Hungarian diesel supplies to Ukraine, greater use of Ukrainian gas storage facilities by Hungarian companies, and joint infrastructure projects, including the opening of new border crossings and a direct rail link between Budapest and Kyiv.

Nevertheless, no formal agreements were signed on Tuesday.

At a subsequent news conference, journalists asked questions about sensitive issues between the two countries: minority rights, Ukraine's EU integration and a new EU loan for Ukraine.

Throughout the day, the two men were visibly keen to avoid any discord.

Magyar, for example, described his angry outburst over Ukraine's "Carpathian Eight" initiative in parliament in late September as a "misunderstanding" and suggested that Hungary might, after all, take part.

Zelenskyy's cautious replies to journalists suggest that he knows his country's path to EU membership also runs through Budapest.

One of Magyar's statements on Tuesday was key: "We've finally put a stop to this completely unnecessary and inexplicable political escalation."

Even before taking office in early May 2026, Magyar had promised to reset relations with Ukraine. But the process has not been entirely smooth.

In many respects — but certainly not all — Magyar is distancing himself from his predecessor. He has made no bones of the fact that he sees Russia as the aggressor, but he rejects both arms deliveries to Ukraine and even the transit of weapons across Hungarian territory.

Magyar previously accused Ukraine of treating ethnic Hungarians as second-class citizens — a claim that is not borne out by the facts. He pressed for greater minority rights and for a time blocked the opening of negotiating chapters in Ukraine's EU accession talks.

Magyar also departed from diplomatic convention by choosing the location of his meeting with Zelenskyy in Ukraine: Indeed, it was Magyar who invited Zelenskyy to Transcarpathia.

Magyar's sometimes confrontational tone toward Ukraine can also be explained by the need to avoid appearing too pro-Ukrainian to the Hungarian public.

According to a November 2026 poll conducted by the think tank Globsec, 33% of Hungarians would now support their country providing military aid to Ukraine. Although this is much more than during Orban's time in office, many Hungarians remain skeptical of Ukraine.

That's why Olena Halushka, a Ukrainian political scientist at the International Centre for Ukrainian Victory (ICUV), sees some aspects of Magyar's visit as a concession to public opinion in Hungary.

"Magyar has taken over a deeply polarized country," she told DW's Ukrainian Service. "A visit to Transcarpathia is more of a step for the Hungarian population than for Ukraine."

Ukraine accommodated not only Magyar's choice of location but also Hungary's demands for better protection of minority rights, which were set out in a 10-point plan in June. That's because EU integration is one of the country's top political priorities.

After planned restrictions on the use of minority languages were withdrawn in late 2023, Ukraine's parliament in early October passed a law on minority language rights that in some respects goes even further than European standards.

Hungary subsequently dropped its obstruction of the opening of negotiating clusters for Ukraine's EU accession.

Laszlo Zubanics, chairman of the Hungarian Democratic Federation in Ukraine (UMDSZ, one of two Hungarian political parties in Transcarpathia), told DW that the Magyar-Zelenskyy meeting was "historic."

He particularly welcomed the fact that Ukraine will probably implement practical improvements in the protection of minority rights "not only by the end of 2027, but much sooner, within just a few months."

A Hungarian diplomat who spoke to DW on condition of anonymity also called the meeting "historic," adding that after the Orban government's anti-Ukrainian policies, trust now needs to be rebuilt, and that personal meetings between the two leaders play an important role in that process.

The diplomat went on to say that Hungary not only wants to ensure that the rights of the Hungarian minority are protected, it also has a strong interest in being involved in Ukraine's reconstruction.

Overall, the diplomat concluded, both sides are very keen to expand economic cooperation.

Hungarian political scientist Daniel Hegedus of the Institute for European Politics (IEP) in Berlin told DW that while the meeting was a "symbolic milestone," it will be important to see "how the two political leaders capitalize on the symbolic political capital generated by this meeting."

No observers have suggested that this is the grand finale of reconciliation between Hungary and Ukraine.

Nevertheless, Tuesday's reset sends an important signal to Europe, namely that if the political will is there, a deep gulf that has existed for years can be transformed into a set of diverging interests that can be addressed through negotiations.

Or, as Zelenskyy put it, now there are "all the opportunities to build hopefully constructive relations."

This article was originally written in German.

#293. Everything to know about Black Friday 2026: Best deals, sale dates, doorbusters, and more

The biggest shopping event of the year is finally here: Black Friday.

Early Black Friday deals started rolling in weeks ago, but now that the actual holiday is upon us, retailers are in deal overload mode. (That will continue through the weekend into Cyber Monday, and likely a few days beyond.) To avoid getting overwhelmed by the hundreds of thousands of deals, it's good to head into the mega-savings event with a plan.

From preparing your shopping list to knowing when the major Black Friday sales start and end, we've got you covered on everything you need to know to shop Black Friday and Cyber Monday.

Almost every major retailer started offering Black Friday deals in early to mid-November. That said, some products have gotten additional price cuts on Black Friday proper, which falls on Nov. 27 in 2026.

Amazon: Amazon's Black Friday Week sale runs from Nov. 19 to 30, offering 12 consecutive days of deals.

Best Buy: Black Friday at Best Buy started on Nov. 19 and runs through Nov. 28. Its Cyber Monday sale runs from Nov. 29 to Nov. 30, followed by a Cyber Week sale that extends savings from Dec. 1 to Dec. 6.

The Home Depot: The Home Depot's Black Friday goes from Nov. 26 to Dec. 2. It will host a Cyber Week sale from Dec. 3 to 6.

Kohl's: The department store's Black Friday Week sale has been live since Nov. 22, and it ends Nov. 28.

Lowe's: Lowe's has a relatively short Black Friday sale compared to other retailers. It runs from Nov. 27 to 30.

Target: Target's Black Friday sale kicked off on Nov. 22 and goes through Nov. 29. Its Cyber Monday sale starts on Nov. 30 at 3 a.m. ET.

Walmart: Walmart is hosting a Black Friday sale from Nov. 23 to Nov. 29 (with deals online only from Nov. 23 to Nov. 26). Its online-only Cyber Monday sale is scheduled for Nov. 30 to Dec. 2.

Absolutely. Amazon's Black Friday deals cover everything from the year's top tech to home essentials. Each day of the sale features new "Today's Big Deals," where select products go on sale for up to 60% off.

On Black Friday and Cyber Monday proper, shoppers get two batches of Big Deals: one at 3 a.m. ET and another at 11 a.m. ET. The last time we checked, featured products currently include the Apple Watch SE 3, Bose QuietComfort Headphones, the Theragun Relief, and the last-gen Echo Dot (which comes with a bonus $25 credit for Prime members).

The Apple Store is hosting a Black Friday Savings Event from Nov. 27 to 30, but it's not offering any product discounts during the sale. Instead, it's just giving away free gift cards worth $25 to $300 with the purchase of select devices and accessories. For the best Black Friday Apple deals that actually save you cash, we recommend shopping at third-party retailers like Amazon, Best Buy, Walmart, and Target instead.

Target has great Black Friday deals if you're looking for toys, Lego sets, Christmas decor, books, or small kitchen appliances. Target's Deal of the Day offers extra savings on hot items, and you can preview upcoming deals several days before they happen. Its Deals of the Day for actual Black Friday take 50% off pajamas and Crocs. Over the weekend, select skincare items, Disney toys, outdoor decor, and shoes will go on sale at deep discounts.

Walmart doesn't skimp on Black Friday deals, and they tend to compete with the best Amazon sales, like $149 Apple AirPods Pro 3. You can also get the Nespresso Vertuo Pop coffee and espresso maker for a rock-bottom price of $59.

It's worth paying close attention to Best Buy's doorbuster deals, in particular. They offer ridiculous savings but tend to sell out quickly (RIP, $149.99 Ninja Slushi). Like Walmart, Best Buy tends to price-match Amazon deals. If you wind up needing a gift in a hurry, Best Buy offers great in-store pickup options as well as quick shipping.

Total and Plus members of the My Best Buy program are eligible to earn double points on their purchases from Nov. 19 to Dec. 6. #292. What OPEC's surprise oil cut means for gas prices

OPEC and its allies’ surprise move to slash oil production will soon be felt at US gas pumps.

The group known as OPEC+ announced Sunday it would cut oil production by more than 1.6 million barrels a day starting in May, running through the end of the year. The news sent both Brent crude futures, the global oil benchmark, and WTI, the US benchmark, up about 6% in trading Monday.

The production cut announcement also had an immediate impact on gasoline futures, which will be passed onto US drivers much more quickly than the spike in oil prices. RBOB, the most closely watched wholesale gasoline price, was up about 8 cents a gallon, or about 3%, in morning trading.

“I think OPEC is reawakening the inflation monster,” said Tom Kloza, global head of energy analysis for OPIS, which tracks gas prices for AAA. “The White House has to be shocked and major-time pissed. It certainly alters the calculus for a while.”

The national average for US gas prices stood at $3.51, on Monday, according to AAA. Kloza said he could see it getting up to $3.80 to $3.90 in relatively short order thanks to the move by OPEC.

“We’re not going to get back to $5 a gallon. I don’t think we’re even going as high as $4,” he said. But he said by the end of the summer US drivers could be back above year-earlier prices, especially if there is a hurricane or other storms affecting production along the Gulf Coast.

The average US regular gas price a year ago stood at $4.19 a gallon in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the disruption that caused to world’s energy markets. Prices eventually reached a record $5.02 a gallon on June 14, before starting a slow but steady decline over the course of more than three months during which the average price fell every day. The decline was partly driven by the release of oil from the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve, and partly by concerns that there could be a US or global recession that reduced the demand for gasoline.

Oil prices surge after OPEC+ producers announce surprise cuts

Even at $3.51, US gas prices were just below the $3.53 average on Feb. 23, 2022, the day before Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

Kloza said one thing keeping prices from getting anywhere near the record levels of 2022 is that the US plans additional releases from the SPR, and US oil production and refining capacity are both up. But a cut of 1 million barrels a day of oil by OPEC+ will not be easy to make up.

“They have ability to cut production and they seem motivated to do so,” he said.

#291. The H3 Podcast is over

On Monday, Hila Klein announced on the show's Instagram account that she had "made the difficult decision to stop working on the new show." She had been developing a crew-led version of the podcast since her estranged husband and co-host, Ethan Klein, was pushed out of it last month after she revealed his affair.

"I've come to realize that I can't continue down this path while also giving myself the space I need to heal and protect my mental health," she wrote. "Right now, I need to focus on myself, my healing, and what's best for me and my kids."

The announcement closes out a month-long fallout that began on Oct. 22. That day, Ethan said on Instagram Stories that the podcast was going on "indefinite hiatus." Hours later, Hila posted that he had been having an affair for more than six months. As Mashable previously reported, the crew said in a statement that they would not keep working with Ethan "involved or profiting in any way." Ethan said he was working to give up his financial stakes in the podcast and in the couple's businesses, including the clothing brand Teddy Fresh.

Complex reported that Hila filed for divorce on Nov. 2, listing their separation date as Oct. 13. The couple married in 2012 and share three children.

Since the news broke, multiple crew members have spoken out. On the show's Discord, longtime producer GirlWithAMicrophone (GWAM) said she would not work on a project with the rest of the crew. She thanked Hila for giving them "a shot during all this turmoil."

Producer AB Ayad suggested on X that the obstacles were bigger than any one person. "There are certain people involved that were never gonna allow us to continue doing the show together," he wrote, adding, "I give Hila a lot of credit that she was able to do what she even did."

Beyond the H3 Podcast, Ethan co-hosted Frenemies with Trisha Paytas, which became one of YouTube's most talked-about shows before it ended acrimoniously in 2021. He later started the political show Leftovers with Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, which ended in 2023 over disagreements about Israel and the war in Gaza.

Since the announcement of the show ending, Ethan has broken his weeks-long silence. On Tuesday, in a series of Instagram Stories, he called the affair "the ultimate betrayal" to his wife and to the show's audience. He also said that "the show ending is entirely my fault."

However, he didn't rule out a comeback. "I will probably be back, but when and how, I can't tell you," he wrote, hinting at a solo show or a new project.

#290. Microdrama apps chase profits as Hollywood moves into short-form, vertical video

Bogdan Nesvit says his mission is simple: "We are essentially building Disney for the 21st century."

Nesvit is the co-founder of microseries app My Drama, built around the latest, bite-sized form of storytelling. Short, serialized "microdrama" videos are created specifically for mobile devices and have generated billions of views this year. They often feature romantic tropes and typically end in cliffhangers to keep viewers hooked.

The category has exploded at a time when traditional media faces waning interest and YouTube now claims more viewing hours than individual streaming platforms.

The microdrama industry is projected to reach $1.5 billion in revenue in the U.S. in 2026, according to research firm Media Partners Asia. In China, where the format originally gained popularity, microdrama revenue surpassed what was made at the box office in 2024.

"It has the potential to evolve into mainstream entertainment and basically become mobile-first video streaming of the size of Netflix," Nesvit said.

Tech companies and startups such as My Drama currently lead the category in metrics like downloads and time spent on the apps.

TikTok's PineDrama is the most popular microdrama app of 2026 so far with 13.2 million U.S. downloads through September, according to Sensor Tower data.

Startups DramaBox and ReelShort beat out entertainment giants Netflix and Disney in average mobile usage time in the U.S. in the third quarter, according to Sensor Tower.

As they see microdramas win over viewers, legacy media companies, Hollywood executives and actors increasingly want in.

Fox Entertainment was one of the earliest Hollywood investors in microdramas. The entertainment studio acquired an equity stake in Holywater Tech, the company behind My Drama, in October 2025.

Fox agreed to produce at least 200 vertical video titles over two years that would be available on the Holywater app. Thus far, hits include dark academia series "Secret Society: Till Blood Do Us Part" and "Kiss of the Pirate King." Individual series have reached tens of millions of views, according to the company.

Nesvit told CNBC in an interview that partnerships like the one between Fox and Holywater benefit studios by providing the infrastructure to publish their short-form videos and get them in front of an audience.

Beyond distributing the videos, Holywater offers advice for what types of content perform best in a short, mobile-first format, according to Nesvit.

"One of the exciting things that we learned when we started talking to studios in Hollywood around two years ago is that all of them are super hungry for consumer data," Nesvit said. "They really want to see how people are interacting with each second of the content."

Nesvit said the company will provide studios with feedback on everything from the length of a camera shot to what color dress a character should wear.

"Our goal is how we can drive audiences from YouTube, from TikTok, from Instagram to our platform, and also create those kinds of synergies [with] legacy media," he said.

Holywater recently adapted Season 3 of Fox's reality TV hit "Farmer Wants a Wife" into a microseries fit for the platform. The company also plans to create a scripted series featuring 30 three-minute episodes inspired by Fox's "Fear Factor: House of Fear."

Holywater currently relies on a combination of subscription fees, which make up about 80% of its revenue, and money from advertisers. Nesvit said the company is also exploring incorporating brand integrations. The company is already profitable, its co-founders said.

Co-founder Anatolii Kasianov said creating the videos is "very cost efficient," with an estimated expense of between $150,000 and $200,000 for an average 70-minute series.

The company's partnerships with content studios, he said, help to bring down customer acquisition costs.

"You attract organically the audience that loves that [intellectual property]," he said.

While Fox saw collaboration as the way into the format, some longtime Hollywood executives are betting they can skip the partnerships and create microdrama platforms in-house.

Jana Winograde, Susan Rovner and Lloyd Braun, who have collectively held leadership roles at NBCUniversal, Showtime, Warner Bros. Discovery and ABC, have jointly founded a microdrama startup called aTwist.

The company, which officially launched in September, has garnered tens of millions of views as of late November across TikTok, Instagram and YouTube, where content lives in addition to the app.

"One of the specialties that we have is really what it means to be a great storyteller," Rovner told CNBC in an interview. "I was president of Warner Bros. Television. I was there for 22 years. During my time there, we had over 18 series go over 100 episodes, so I definitely think we have an expertise in getting people to care about these shows, care about the characters, invest."

"A lot of our competitors' completion rates are very low, their churn rates are very high," Rovner said. "They can often bring people into the store but they can't keep them."

The average churn rate for the most downloaded microdrama apps is nearly 60% so far in 2026, according to Sensor Tower data. The market intelligence firm notes that the number of users lost in each quarter this year has roughly equaled the number of users gained.

ATwist seeks to keep viewers enticed through high-stakes, compelling characters and unique stories. The app has already ordered second seasons of shows and puts a particular emphasis on talent, according to the co-founders.

Jesse Tyler Ferguson, known for his role as Mitchell on "Modern Family," and his husband, Justin Mikita, a Broadway producer, have collaborated on the musical series "Theater Kids vs. Zombies" for aTwist. It premiered on Oct. 15.

Other series that debuted last month included "Honey, I Think Our House Is Haunted" starring Mario Lopez and "Unboxing the Killer Doll" starring Paris Hilton.

In May, aTwist announced an exclusive partnership with Skydance's linear television channel BET to create horizontal microdramas that air first on BET and later stream in vertical format on aTwist's app.

"That brings a lot of awareness to our brand, a lot of marketing," Winograde said. "But it also gives these linear networks the opportunity to get programming at an incredibly low cost that, from what we're seeing, the audience loves."

Winograde suggested aTwist could strike similar partnerships in the future.

Large streaming companies, which have already faced competition from social media apps and YouTube, are exploring ways to incorporate microdramas inside their existing apps.

NBCUniversal's Peacock launched its own vertical video channel within the app this summer that features both original unscripted series and more traditional vertical dramas. NBCUniversal is also eyeing international development by investing in an Indian microdrama platform, EloElo Group's Story TV, earlier this month.

"At NBCUniversal, we see significant opportunity in mobile-first storytelling and emerging formats like microdramas to engage audiences and meet evolving viewing habits," Deepak Arya, executive vice president for corporate strategy and development at NBCUniversal, said in a press release.

Disney+, Paramount+ and Netflix similarly launched vertical channels embedded in their services this year. Notably, the channels are meant to help viewers discover traditional content and so far haven't featured original, vertical-first series.

On top of those media companies, head of Prime Video and Amazon MGM Studios Mike Hopkins told CNBC's Julia Boorstin in an interview last month that the tech company was interested in producing its own microdramas.

Despite the flurry of investment, Hollywood still faces the challenge of how to translate viewing hours into profit, especially for shorter content.

Leading U.S. microdrama app ReelShort posted a net loss of $12 million in 2025 despite bringing in total revenue of $785 million, according to research compiled by Media Partners Asia, or MPA.

The app, which was founded in 2022 by California-based Crazy Maple Studio, currently reaches about 65 million users every month, according to the company's LinkedIn profile.

However, high marketing and content costs have weighed on the company's bottom line. MPA expects ReelShort to reach profitability for the first time this year, with an estimated $40 million in net profit.

Media Partners Asia CEO Vivek Couto told CNBC that acquiring new users is the largest cost, with ReelShort spending an estimated 55% of its revenue in 2025 on marketing.

Couto also noted high content spend, especially since microdrama apps typically require a high volume of content.

"The content is very hit-driven … it wears out fast," Couto said. "The churn rate for this sector is high, so you have to fill that slate all the time, and you have to win back those users."

Correction: A previous version misstated Holywater Tech's full name in first reference. Co-founder Anatolii Kasianov also said expenses run between $150,000 and $200,000 for an average 70-minute series. A previous version misstated the average series length.

Updated November 27, 2026: More walking pad and running treadmill deals were added. Prices and links were also updated.

The Urevo CyberPad is my favorite walking pad, and it’s on sale for $390 ($110 off). I’m confident in the product’s durability, mainly due to its sturdy-feeling build and comfortable belt. This might appeal to folks who enjoy gamifying their workouts, though. The app also offers workout programs that auto-adjust the speed to your pace via sensors under the belt.

#287. Can Rassvet, 'Russia's Starlink' change the course of the war in Ukraine?

SpaceX's US Starlink satellite system has played a key role in countering the Russian military in Ukraine, but now a Russian counterpart is under development. What could this mean for Ukraine?

Both Russian and international media refer to the satellite communications network Rassvet (Dawn) as the "Russian Starlink," a satellite internet service operated by the US company SpaceX.

Rassvet, which was developed by the Russian aerospace company Bureau 1440, operates in low Earth orbit.

Interest in the system surged after the Russian military lost access to Starlink terminals, which until then had ensured communications and internet access in the battle zone in Ukraine.On the front, for example, Starlink helps drone pilots and commanders receive images from drones equipped with cameras. Military personnel also communicate together thanks to Starlink.

Though Russia does not fall within Starlink's area of coverage, the Russian military managed to acquire "illegal" terminals through third countries and was thus using the same system as the Ukrainian army.

In early 2026, SpaceX, in coordination with the Ukrainian Defense Ministry, introduced a "whitelist," which registered all devices on Ukrainian territory authorized to operate on the Starlink network. Any terminals being used by Russian forces were subsequently deactivated, and reports of serious communication problems on the front then began to appear in Russian social media channels.

In May, the US news channel Bloomberg reported that the Ukrainian army had recaptured about 400 square kilometers (ca. 155 square miles) of Ukrainian territory since Russian forces lost access to Starlink.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Two first launches of serial Rassvet satellites took place in March and July 2026.

According to information from Ukraine's military intelligence (HUR) published by the Reuters news agency in early November, Russia has started using Rassvet for military communications over Ukraine and to carry out attacks.

The system is reportedly being used to improve strike accuracy, expand capabilities of reconnaissance drones and to strengthen resilience against electronic warfare.

HUR spokesperson Andriy Yusov also told Reuters that "the constellation is currently insufficient to provide uninterrupted coverage of Ukrainian territory."

Georgiy Trishkin, a rocket analyst and operator of Telegram channel Tekhassky Vestnik (The Texas Herald), told DW that Russia aims to have a functioning "sovereign" alternative to Starlink — consisting of 292 satellites in orbit — running by the end of 2027.

According to Serhii Beskrestnov, aka Flash, an advisor to the Ukrainian president, the main danger posed by the Rassvet system is that it could allow the Russian army to control drones over Ukrainian territory.

He also pointed out on the platform Facebook that the Ukrainian military cannot use Starlink to control drones over Russian territory, since the US service does not work there.

Inspired by the Starlink model, the Russian military also wants to be able to equip drones with terminals, which will enable connectivity in more remote parts of Ukrainian territory. Bureau 1440 unveiled some initial models last month, but according to Trishkin, the similarities between Rassvet and Starlink stop at the "basic features and concept."

"When it comes to details, these are completely different projects. No one can currently match SpaceX's technological edge — and especially its lead in production technology," he said, pointing out that while the Starlink constellation comprised over 10,000 satellites, Rassvet would not have more than 300 in its first phase.

He added that Bureau 1440 would struggle to make enough of the kits used on the ground. While SpaceX can manufacture about 15,000 per day, this would be a "remarkable achievement even over the course of a year" for the Russian company.

He also said that the terminals produced by Bureau 1440 were much more expensive than those by Starlink as they relied "on foreign components."

"Right now, no one can beat SpaceX in terms of price, volume and quality of service," Trishkin said. "The next step for the company is mobile satellite services, where it's making very rapid progress. Will Bureau 1440 be able to respond? Unlikely for the time being."

SpaceX's Starlink was primarily designed as a civilian service, while Starshield is more for government and military sectors.

According to DW sources, Rassvet was likely designed to support battlefield communications and thus does not currently require as many satellites as Starlink.

Ukrainian military expert Oleh Starikov said that if Rassvet continues to develop as it has then it could fulfil the mission put to it by the Russian military. He added that SpaceX CEO Elon Musk was developing a system that would work around the world, whereas Bureau 1440's satellites sufficed for Russian military purposes.

But he also underlined the massive expansion of Russia's satellite network generally, which — on January 1, 2022, before the full-scale invasion of Ukraine — comprised 102 satellites according to Dmitry Rogozin, who at the time was general director of the Russian space agency Roscosmos.

In September of this year, Rogozin's successor Dmitry Bakanov said that the number almost quadrupled.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Recent restrictions to Starlink services in Ukraine have brought the issue to the fore again. In mid-November, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that Starshield had been throttled in Ukraine.

"Unfortunately, our units have been recording significant disruptions to Starshield's operations over the territory of Ukraine for several days now — along the entire front line and in the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine," he said, adding that the restrictions occurred at speeds of 161 km/h and higher.

Restrictions on the use of Starlink were first put in place on October 14 and then lifted, according to US President Donald Trump, on October 23.

When asked by DW whether the Ukrainian military could gain access to Rassvet, Trishkin said it was "only a matter of time" before terminals fell "into foreign hands and are subsequently examined."

This article was originally written in Russian.

#286. Inflation has shoppers hunting for value. That bodes well for Black Friday

Economic headwinds have made consumers more cautious — but new data and reports from retailers are painting a picture of robust holiday spending through Black Friday and beyond.

The macroeconomic environment has squeezed wallets. High inflation, fluctuating gas prices and labor uncertainty have dampened consumer sentiment and contributed to a pullback in spending. October's consumer price index rose a seasonally adjusted 0.4%, coming in higher than expected, while the personal consumption expenditures price index accelerated to a seasonally adjusted 3.8% in October compared with last year. Meanwhile, October retail sales grew at their slowest pace in nearly a year, according to the CNBC/NRF Retail Monitor.

The Conference Board's Consumer Confidence Index slid to its lowest since 2014 in September, with respondents citing concerns about inflation and the job market. It's translated into caution from some retailers like Walmart and Lowe's, which have reported slower sales, smaller baskets and drops in big-ticket and discretionary purchases.

Despite that pullback, recent earnings reports and end-of-year forecasts suggest consumers are still willing to shell out for the holidays.

Planned spending on gifts and nongifts is estimated to be $1,049 on average this year, up 5.9% from $990 last year, according to The Conference Board. Adjusting for inflation, that figure is still up 3.2% year over year.

Holiday sales are expected to top $1 trillion this year, but that growth is boosted by inflation. Though consumers have said they're willing to spend, experts have noted that shoppers are still emphasizing value and looking for deals where they can. Adobe data found that in the first 22 days of November — what it considers the beginning of the holiday season — consumers spent $82.5 billion online, marking a 9.1% year-over-year increase.

That's translating to the Black Friday and Cyber Monday week, too, as consumers take advantage of deals that started days before the traditional Friday blitz. Salesforce is predicting a record-breaking holiday week between Nov. 24 and Nov. 30, as it expects online sales to reach $357 billion globally and $84 billion in the U.S., both marking 6% year-over-year increases.

The report also found that retailers are offering bigger markdowns than last year, with discount rates up 8% in the U.S. in November.

And according to Deloitte's Black Friday survey, participation in the shopping holiday this year is expected to be the highest seen since 2016, with 87% of shoppers reporting they plan to buy during Black Friday and Cyber Monday sales.

That number is up from 82% in 2025. Consumers are expecting to spend an average of $624 this holiday, similar to last year's numbers, and Generation Z is going all in on those deals, according to Deloitte, which surveyed 1,200 consumers in mid-October. That echoes similar behavior from the cohort last year.

"It's sort of the mix of feeling the squeeze on prices, people thinking about their economic condition and their financial position, but still wanting to protect the holidays," Brian McCarthy, retail strategy lead at Deloitte, told CNBC in an interview.

He added that even as shoppers pulled back on spending over the past few months and delayed big purchases, that spend is now being more heavily concentrated into promotional windows like the holiday season. They're searching for more deals, becoming more savvy and deferring some spending.

The Deloitte data also found that 40% of Gen Z shoppers plan to use buy now, pay later for their shopping this holiday season.

"People do care about the holidays and want to make sure they can buy those gifts to share with their friends and family, but it's another way of deferring when they're going to have to pay for that item," McCarthy said.

On the other side of the cash register, retailers are expecting similar holiday shopping behavior and reported optimism about the consumer in earnings reports over the past two weeks.

Walmart CFO John David Rainey told CNBC last week that the company is continuing to see a resilient consumer. The retailer is leaning into value with rollbacks and deals, and Rainey said the holiday quarter was "off to a pretty good start" as macroeconomic trends start to show signs of potential improvement.

"The fact remains that payrolls are healthy, the equity markets are holding up in the face of geopolitical uncertainty, and even though consumer sentiment is somewhat lower, it hasn't translated into reduced economic output," Rainey said.

Target executives also said last week that the retailer is optimistic about holiday spending this season. The company is pricing thousands of products at $5 and under and investing in elevated products while prioritizing low prices, they said.

"We're encouraged by the start of the quarter that we've seen so far," CEO Michael Fiddelke told reporters following the company's third-quarter earnings report. "We're really excited for what guests are going to find at Target this holiday season."

Best Buy CEO Jason Bonfig told CNBC on Tuesday that while the company is seeing consumers place higher emphasis on value, those shoppers are also looking to upgrade products, sometimes into "more premium price points."

Lowe's is also expecting a solid holiday season, with CEO Marvin Ellison telling CNBC last week that the company's November sales to date are in line with its expectations. The home improvement company is also emphasizing deals for customers who may be more price-conscious, but Ellison said he's still "optimistic."

Executives at TJX Companies, a retailer known for its value proposition, said on an earnings call with analysts last week that the company is expecting sales momentum to accelerate throughout the holiday season.

"In the current environment, we believe value will be top of mind for many consumers this holiday season," CEO Ernie Herrman said on the call.

Still, TJX said warmer weather in the beginning of the fourth quarter led to a sales slowdown. The company also reported weak fourth-quarter guidance, coming in below Wall Street expectations for earnings and same-store sales. Competitor Burlington Stores also posted weak sales and provided a lower-than-expected outlook.

Gap Inc. saw a similar trend. CEO Richard Dickson told CNBC that the company's sales lagged at the beginning of the quarter due to warmer weather. The retailer posted flat comparable sales for its fiscal third quarter last week and reported sinking sales at its Athleta and Banana Republic banners. It also lowered its guidance.

But Dickson said the retailer is optimistic about colder weather beginning to drive spending again.

"We're entering the peak holiday season and selling weeks with pent-up demand and hopefully maintained good weather for shopping," Dickson said. "This could be, and would be, a source of upside."

#283. Scientists film deepest ever fish on seabed off Japan

Sign up for CNN’s Wonder Theory science newsletter. Explore the universe with news on fascinating discoveries, scientific advancements and more.

Cruising at a depth of 8,336 meters (over 27,000 feet) just above the seabed, a young snailfish has become the deepest fish ever filmed by scientists during a probe into the abyss of the northern Pacific Ocean.

Scientists from University of Western Australia and Tokyo University of Marine Science and Technology released footage of the snailfish on Sunday filmed last September by sea robots in deep trenches off Japan.

Along with the filming the deepest snailfish, the scientists physically caught two other specimens at 8,022 meters and set another record for the deepest catch.

Previously, the deepest snailfish ever spotted was at 7,703 meters in 2008, while scientists had never been able to collect fish from anywhere below 8,000 meters.

“What is significant is that it shows how far a particular type of fish will descend in the ocean,” said marine biologist Alan Jamieson, founder of the Minderoo-UWA Deep Sea Research Centre, who led the expedition.

Scientists are filming in the trenches off Japan as part of a 10-year study into the deepest fish populations in the world. Snailfish are members of Liparidae family, and while most snailfish live in shallow water, others survive at some of the greatest depths ever recorded, Jamieson said.

During the two-month survey last year, three “landers” – automatic sea robots fitted with high-resolution cameras – were dropped into three trenches – the Japan, Izu-Ogasawara and Ryukyu trenches – at varying depths.

In the Izu-Ogasawara trench, footage showed the deepest snailfish hovering calmly alongside other crustaceans on the seabed.

Jamieson classified the fish as a juvenile and said younger deep sea snailfish often stay as deep as possible to avoid being eaten by bigger predators that swim at shallower depths.

Another clip shot at between 7,500 and 8,200 meters in the same trench showed a colony of fish and crustaceans munching at bait tied to an undersea robot.

Images of the two captured snailfish – identified as Pseudoliparis belyaevi – provide a rare glimpse of the unique features that help the deep sea species survive the extreme environment.

They have tiny eyes, a translucent body, and their lack of swim bladder, which helps other fish float, works to their advantage, Jamieson said.

The professor said the Pacific Ocean is particularly conducive to vibrant activity due to its warm southern current, which encourages sea creatures to go deeper, while its abundant marine life provides a good source of food for bottom feeders.

Scientists would like to know more about creatures living at extreme depths, but cost is the constraint, Jamieson said, adding that each lander alone costs them $200,000 to assemble and operate.

“The challenges are that technology has been expensive and scientists don’t have a lot of money,” he said.

Apple gear goes hand-in-hand with holiday sales. WIRED readers love opportunities to save on MacBooks, iPads, AirPods, and other gadgets—and while discounts on Apple products aren't especially rare, Black Friday deals do usually drop these sought-after items to their lowest prices of the year.

I've rounded up the best discounts on Apple products and accessories below. Everything you see has been hand-tested by someone on the WIRED Reviews team, and every price has been hand-checked ahead of publishing. We'll keep this story updated throughout the weekend.

AirPods Pro 3 are finally, actually on sale. The best wireless earbuds for iPhone owners are usually slightly discounted, but this Black Friday price is a truly good deal worth considering if you're in the market for an earbud upgrade. They're comfortable, have great noise cancelation, and have never been this cheap before.

For over-ear headphone enthusiasts looking to keep thing Apple, the AirPods Max 2 are the best option thanks to their clear sound and top-notch noise cancelation. They're also eye-wateringly expensive and basically never drop very far in price. If you've been hemming and hawing trying to figure out a smart time to buy, we think it's right now.

We especially like these earbuds for working out. They fit around your ear so they'll stay in place while running—something AirPods definitely do not do (at least not for me). They have punchy sound and solid noise cancelation, plus dust and water resistance.

We love this MacBook and think it's the best option for most people looking to buy a laptop of any kind. The only real drawback is its price, but at $250 off for Black Friday, now is a great time to buy. It strikes a balance between price and performance that WIRED editor Luke Larsen calls “unbeatable,” and it manages to do it in a sleek, high-quality build that inspires confidence.

The inexpensive MacBook Neo doesn't drop in price very often, but Black Friday has shaved just a bit off the top ($50). We wish it had more RAM, but otherwise, the Neo is totally adequate for most basic use cases: think internet browsing, office software, video calls, and watching your favorite shows.

The base iPad is the model we recommend most often, and while it is no stranger to sales, it's absolutely worth considering if you're thinking about getting someone an iPad as a gift. It isn't powerful enough to be a work machine, but for browsing, content streaming, and “games on your phone,” it'll do the trick.

In my personal and professional opinion, the Apple AirTag doesn't get enough love. I became an AirTag enthusiast this year and now I have one on my keys, in my car, in my purse, and on my luggage. The four-pack price isn't as enticing as it could be, but picking up a single AirTag for under $20 is a steal. The batteries are replaceable and the Bluetooth tracker can play a loud chime if you're looking for it and can't find it.

You can never have enough wall chargers. This option is tiny and comes in colors that match with many iPhones. It has folding prongs and a single USB-C port. I always keep one around for when my power bank inevitably dies.

This MagSafe AirPods case is rugged and protective, with a magnetic closure that keeps your earbuds extra protected. The optional lanyard comes in handy if you don't have space to spare in your bag or pockets.

This MagSafe wallet doubles as a tripod and is great to have around for emergency fit checks or group photos. I also like it for hands-free FaceTime calls. There's a version with Apple Find My compatibility that is also slightly discounted.

MagSafe wallets can be tricky to use, but this one makes it easy to get your cards out. Simply press them in and the wallet's mechanism will pop them out for you to grab. The look isn't that special, but the functionality can't be beat.

#280. Data centers are getting their own natural gas power plants

The numbers behind the off-grid gas power boom.

One of the biggest roadblocks to starting up a data center is getting approval to connect to the electric grid—a wait that could last as long as a decade. Some developers aren’t willing to wait and are instead opting to build their own off-grid, or behind-the-meter, gas power plants to fuel the AI boom.

xAI’s Memphis campus has famously used dozens of natural gas turbines, some of them without permits, as far back as 2024. At the time, that facility was a rarity, and it faced scrutiny from regulators. It remains the subject of ongoing legal battles. But the strategy of going off-grid for power has since become a lot more common.

As of October 2026, data center developers have announced plans for more than 100 behind-the-meter gas power plants at facilities in the US, according to data from Cleanview, a market intelligence company. The facilities have a combined planned capacity of over 115 gigawatts, more than double the peak power demand of California. The vast majority of these announcements have come since the beginning of 2025.

It’s possible that not all these facilities will be built; only a small fraction are under construction or operating today. But there’s a growing trend of large data centers looking to build their own power supply, and this could shape the grid—and its climate impacts—for decades to come.

Building your own power plant is generally more expensive than just hooking up to the grid, but the AI rush has made developers willing to pay a significant premium to get online faster. “The biggest motivator for on-site power right now from data centers is speed,” says Musfika Mishi, an associate at BloombergNEF, an energy consultancy.

When developers want to build a new industrial facility—like a data center—that requires a lot of electricity, they need to request a grid connection from a local utility or regional grid operator. That request kicks off a yearslong process in which grid planners study the existing grid to understand what would need to be built to safely deliver power to the facility without compromising reliability. Upgrades might be required, like building new transmission lines or larger transformers, and the developer might be on the hook to help pay for them.

Rather than waiting for that process to play out, developers can opt to instead build their own power plants. These facilities are referred to as “behind the meter” because they sit on the customer’s side of a utility meter—supplying the building directly, rather than relying on a utility via a grid hookup.

“This shift in the data center developers’ power strategies towards off-grid gas raises some important questions about how data centers will be powered going forward,” says Brendan Pierpont, director of electricity at the think tank Energy Innovation.

Behind-the-meter doesn’t always mean being totally disconnected from the grid, however. Some facilities may build such plants as a temporary measure, eventually connecting to the grid and tapping their own power plants only as backup. “It’s really just a very expensive way to bridge that maybe five-to-seven-year timeline gap until these data centers can get a grid connection,” Pierpont says.

Even if gas plants are pitched as a near-term solution, building new fossil fuel infrastructure could lead to longer-term effects, since an operator might choose to continue running plants once they’ve spent money building them. “Even though data centers say that it’s a grid-bridging solution, the probability that it is going to be in use much longer is a real risk, and that leads to fossil fuel lock-in,” Mishi says.

The on-site gas rush could have major implications for greenhouse-gas emissions. Today, the US grid is still reliant on fossil fuels, but nuclear and renewables together make up about 40% of electricity generation. That means making a grid connection is generally a lower-emissions option than relying entirely on an on-site gas plant. (That’s not the case everywhere—India, for example, is expecting to see a data center boom in the next decade, and its grid is largely served by emissions-intensive coal-fired power plants today.)

Utilities are already planning to build more natural gas power plants on the grid to meet rising electricity demand. Equipment manufacturers are struggling to keep up with the surge, and it’s pushing developers of behind-the-meter plants toward less-efficient alternatives.

Today, large natural gas plants generally use combined-cycle turbines. These capture heat to generate additional electricity, making them more efficient than single-cycle turbines, which are generally cheaper to build. Very few of the planned behind-the-meter facilities, however, will use combined-cycle turbines, Mishi says. That means these off-grid plants will likely produce more greenhouse-gas emissions than even other natural gas resources.

BloombergNEF is also tracking on-site natural gas plants at data centers, finding 181 gigawatts’ worth of announced projects globally, with 90% of that capacity designated for the US. If all planned behind-the-meter gas plants for data centers in the US go ahead, they could emit 345 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent each year by 2035, according to a BloombergNEF report. That’s 152 million metric tons more than if those data centers pulled power from the US grid—a difference greater than the total annual emissions of the Netherlands.

And while it might seem logical that data centers bringing their own power could ease communities’ energy bills, those facilities going off-grid doesn’t protect prices for everyone else, says Matthias Fripp, director of global policy research at Energy Innovation. More demand for natural gas could push its price higher, he explains, which could in turn raise rates for the roughly 60% of American households that use natural gas for heating and cooking. That effect may also trickle into electricity prices.

There’s still a lot of uncertainty about how much of this gas rush will come to fruition, so this future isn’t set in stone. Today, just 4.9 gigawatts of behind-the-meter gas projects tied to data centers are operating, and 15.8 gigawatts are under construction, according to Cleanview’s data.

Creative solutions could also help limit the climate burden of the on-site gas buildout, BloombergNEF’s Mishi says. Building gas alongside on-site renewables or energy storage could help limit how often a gas plant needs to fire up, she says, though the economics of building multiple energy sources can be tricky.

While the grid is struggling to keep up with demand, building more renewables could help, Fripp adds. In a recent study, his team found that building renewables and energy storage to meet rising electricity demand could be reliable and cheaper than relying on fossil fuels.

“These data centers want a lot of power, and they want it fast, and the grid is not well equipped to provide that,” Fripp says. “There are potentially good solutions and bad solutions … Rushing off the grid and putting in your own behind-the-meter gas is probably a bad way, because it’s still going to raise other people’s bills, and it’s not great for the environment.”

These scientists hope that fire-spotting satellites, AI tools and ancient land practices could preserve the world’s vulnerable permafrost—and the vast carbon it stores.

New technology could help cut power losses and reinvent a staple of the grid.

Batteries that swap liquid electrolytes for solid materials promise to charge faster, last longer, and (crucially) run cooler.

#279. Russia-Ukraine war extends to the Baltic and the Mediterranean

By attacking Russian vessels around the world, Ukraine is trying to increase the pressure on Russia and also sending out signals to its Western allies. What is the impact on global maritime trade?

First there was an attack on a Russian cargo vessel, the Sparta II, off the Finnish coast, then on the Russian corvette Merkury and a dry cargo vessel that was allegedly carrying weapons off the coast of Libya. These spectacular Ukrainian operations in regions far from the Ukrainian capital Kyiv have caused a stir. They came shortly after several suspected Russian missiles crashed in Poland, not far from where an international military exercise was underway.

Intelligence agencies have long warned that Russia was preparing some form of provocation along NATO's eastern flank.

What are the risks of Russia's war in Ukraine escalating further and drawing in other regions?

It is no secret that Russia has long since expanded its operations beyond Ukraine: With military provocation, hybrid operations and acts of sabotage, Moscow has attempted to put pressure on the countries that openly support Ukraine.

And Ukraine has also targeted Russia's military and economy beyond its borders.

Since the summer, attacks by both Russia and Ukraine have increased in the Black Sea. Not only have Russian and Ukrainian cargo ships been targeted, but also vessels from other countries, particularly Turkey.

Furthermore, in the past few years, Ukraine has managed to deal significant blows to Russia, deep within Russian territory, thanks to aerial and maritime drones. It has targeted military airfields and other strategic targets such as oil refineries, including one in Omsk, Siberia, as well as military vessels in the eastern Black Sea.

Russia has access only to a very narrow strip of the Baltic Sea coast, which is flanked by Finland and Estonia. Even ahead of the attack on the Sparta II, Ukraine had struck in the area multiple times, targeting oil terminals in the region around St. Petersburg, in Ust-Luga and Primorsk.

Russia uses the Baltic Sea to transport supplies to its Kaliningrad exclave and to export oil and other goods to the rest of the world, with the help of its "shadow fleet."

Ukrainian special forces are also said to have carried out operations against Russian military facilities in Syria, well before the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024. They are also reported to have lent support to local Tuareg fighters in Mali who were able to inflict heavy losses on the Malian army and allied Russian mercenaries.

Kyiv is thus attempting to harm Russia's military and economy worldwide, even if in military terms this does not help Ukraine directly.

The Russian corvette that was sunk was part of Russia's Black Sea Fleet but because of Turkey's blockade of the Bosporus and the Dardanelles, it would not have been allowed to return to the Black Sea. Instead, it was escorting Russian cargo ships in the Mediterranean. Primarily, the attacks send a political message: Russian ships can no longer feel safe — anywhere in the world.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

"We are not speaking about random shadow vessels which simply transport oil above the price cap and as a result bring revenues for the Russian treasury," security expert Elisabeth Braw from the Atlantic Council told DW. Sparta II was suspected of carrying military equipment, which Moscow denies.

"Ukraine is showing that it knows exactly, and secondly that it's able to hit them wherever and whatever waters they are in," Braw continued. "And this is something I don't think Ukraine has been able to do at the beginning of the war."

Officially, Kyiv's goal is to disrupt Russian logistics and supply routes, but military experts and politicians also see the attacks as a clear political signal to Western allies. They suspect that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is sending a clear message of strength with an eye toward possible future peace negotiations.

In an interview on the German news outlet Tagesschau, security expert Joachim Weber from the University of Bonn suggested that Zelenskyy was paying less attention to the US, out of a sense of disappointment. He said that Ukrainian attacks in distant maritime areas were a sign that there was less inhibition and that Ukraine was ready to expand the conflict geographically to increase pressure on Russia, despite the risks.

Weber warned that war could become omnipresent if there was an increase in attacks on civilian vessels or ships that were considered suspicious in international waters. He said that Russia was providing more military escorts for the ships of its shadow fleet. "The likelihood that an accidental exchange of fire between armed forces, coast guards or anyone could occur is rising."

Braw pointed out that violations of the Law of the Sea were not only rising with regard to the Russia-Ukraine war but also in relation to other conflicts and playing out in "the South China Sea, the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea."

She said about 90% of global trade today was conducted via the oceans and she feared that others might conclude it was not "really to their advantage" to follow the rules of international maritime law.

She added that they might find it "beneficial in the short term to violate maritime rules" for short-term gains. "That would make the world's oceans significantly less safe for everybody."

This article was originally written in German.
