#278. What pet cemeteries reveal about being human

Editor’s Note:  Eric Tourigny is a lecturer in historical archaeology at Newcastle University, UK. His research interprets osteological and material culture remains alongside historic texts to examine changing human-animal relationships in Europe and North America over the past 500 years. The views expressed in this commentary are his own. Read more opinion on CNN.

Why do we bury our departed loved ones in a cemetery? A primary purpose is to provide survivors with an opportunity to grieve and gain a sense of closure. The cemetery is a place for the living as much as it is a place for the dead.

But what about when the dearly departed are not human – but our pets?

The Spanish city of Barcelona recently announced that it will be investing in the establishment of the country’s first public pet cemetery. Set to open next year, it will offer both burials and cremations – with an estimated 7,000 carried out each year.

For me, as someone who has spent years researching the development of pet cemeteries elsewhere in the world, this news came as a shock. Barcelona is a densely populated city with limited privately owned land – one where 50% of families own a pet.

How did a city that is home to 180,000 dogs not already have a public pet cemetery? Until now, the service was only provided by the private sector, according to Barcelona’s Councilor for Climate Emergency and Ecological Transition, Eloi Badia. He added that the municipal-funded initiative was sparked by “constant public demand.”

After all, public pet cemeteries have been around in Europe and the Americas since the late 19th century. Britain’s first public pet cemetery appeared in London’s Hyde Park in 1881. New York’s Hartsdale pet cemetery was founded in 1896, followed a few years later by Paris’ ornate Cimetière des Chiens in 1899.

I became interested in the history of modern pet burial practices while investigating the archaeological record of a centuries-old house in Toronto. I came across a (very) large dog buried in the back garden which, according to the historical record, was occupied between 1840 and 1870.

This dog survived to an elderly age but, sadly, suffered from degenerative joint disease and severe infections during his last months. His ailments progressed to such a state that suggest he received some level of care in his final weeks. He then was buried in a personal plot behind the family home.

This elderly dog led me to think about the different ways people interact with the bodies of their pets after death. Could this behavior be reflective of the relationships they held with their animals in life? In this instance, why take the time to carefully bury a dog in its own space when other, arguably easier options existed?

This, after all, was an era when people often disposed of their dead pets in the river, or might have sold their bodies for meat and skin.

Good hygiene is an obvious reason to choose a burial – no one wants decomposing animal bodies in the street or their garden – but that wouldn’t immediately warrant a personalized, dedicated burial and gravestone.

The most straight forward option would be to dispose of a deceased animal with the household waste. But such treatment would evidently feel less ceremonious and would not offer appropriate emotional closure to what was likely an important relationship.

Like the burial of people, the burial of pets is an intimate cultural practice, one that changes over time and is reflective of the changing relationships that a society has with its cherished creatures.

My study of historic gravestones and epitaphs in Britain from the Victorian period to today shows this changing human-animal relationship. In the 19th century, gravestones were often dedicated to a “loving friend” or “devoted companion,” suggesting pets were mostly considered important friends.

By the early 20th century, pets had become members of the family – evidenced by the appearance of family surnames on the gravestones, and loving epitaphs written by “Mummy and Daddy.”

By the early 20th century, pets had become members of the family – evidenced by the appearance of family surnames on the gravestones, and loving epitaphs written by “Mummy and Daddy.”

Society’s changing attitude towards the role of animals in the afterlife can also be found. Fast-forward a few decades later, and gravestones were more likely to reference a reunion then earlier ones. For example, the owners of Denny, the “brave little cat” buried in an east London cemetery in 1952, wrote on his epitaph “God bless until we meet again.”

I wonder what the epitaphs in Barcelona’s new cemetery will reveal about modern Catalan relationships with animals.

Over time, our ways of treating our animal dead appear to reflect an even closer relationship in life. Once strictly forbidden by law, the last decade saw many jurisdictions, like the state of New York, allowing the co-burial of cremated animals and people, which will undoubtedly lead to changing funerary and commemoration practices for both humans and animals.

For me, the most remarkable similarity between modern and historic pet cemeteries is the striking evidence for the heartbreak and taboos around grieving for animals.

The connection that someone has with their pet can be just as strong and just as significant as their relationships with other humans. Yet today, as in over 100 years ago, individuals continue to struggle to find the appropriate outlet to express their pain, hiding heartache for fear of the social repercussions that might come with public acknowledgment of the existence of such a bond.

The RSPCA reassures the public on its website that they should not feel shame for their grief. In the UK, charities like the Blue Cross and Rainbow Bridge Pet Loss Grief Center offer counseling to bereaved humans.

Close relationships between people and animals have existed for millennia, but in western European cultures, there were few acceptable ways to mourn that relationship. As society becomes more accepting of the importance of human-animal relationships to our collective wellbeing, it is not surprising to see us follow rituals resembling those we use to mourn the loss of our closest human relationships.

At an estimated cost of €200 ($217) per service at the new Barcelona cemetery, it is important to acknowledge that this opportunity to grieve will not be financially available to everyone in the city.

This will not be a space for all of the city’s pets. Pet owners may opt to keep cremated remains within their home or spread out ashes in a meaningful location instead. Online forums and digital pet cemeteries also provide other opportunities to commemorate the relationship and express grief.

Whether one chooses a pet cemetery or not, there are many acceptable ways to express your grief – and to remember your relationship with the important animals in your life.

#274. Germany: 2 arrested, suspected of plotting synagogue attack

Federal prosecutors say they have ordered the arrest of two members of a pro-Iranian group on suspicion of planning an attack on a synagogue. They were detained in the cities of Heidelberg and Cologne.

Germany's federal prosecutor's office on Thursday said it had ordered the arrest of two Iraqi citizens in Germany who are believed to be members of a pro-Iranian terrorist group.

It identified the men as Mostafa Al-R. and Ameer J., and said that they were arrested in Heidelberg in Baden-Württemberg in the southwest, and in Cologne, several hours' drive to the north.

Officers from Germany's federal criminal police force carried out the arrests.

Prosecutors also announced searches and raids of 17 sites in total across three separate states, saying these were ongoing.

After two suspects were arrested, Hendrik Wüst, the premier of North Rhine-Westphalia, thanked the security agencies for their vigilance and dedication. "Protecting Jewish life is our shared responsibility," he wrote on X.

"Jewish life must be able to flourish freely and safely in our country. Anyone who attacks it attacks us all," Wüst added.

Prosecutors said the two men were "strongly suspected" of membership in a domestic terrorist organization.

They said that Mostafa Al-R. wa an associate of a man in the US known as Mohammad Al-Saadi, who is accused of setting up a group with the acronym HAYI (Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiyya) that is thought to be "responsible for a series of attacks against US, Israeli and Jewish institutions in Europe from March 2026," in the aftermath of the outbreak of Donald Trump's war with Iran.

Mostafa Al-R. and Al-Saadi allegedly "founded a separate organization to prepare and carry out further attacks in Germany and Europe at the end of 2025."

Prosecutors say Ameer J. joined this group. It gathered funds and "recruited several external people to carry out explosive attacks."

"On the group's orders, unknown assailants headed on two consecutive nights in late March 2026 — presumably with explosives — to synagogues in Cologne and in one other European city," prosecutors wrote. "The plan was, for reasons as yet unknown, ultimately not carried out."

Prosecutors said that intelligence behind the arrests could be traced back to the federal domestic intelligence agency, the BfV.

More than 250 police officers from various forces were part of Thursday's operation.

Both suspects were expected to appear before judges later on Thursday for a decision on them being placed in investigative detention.

One other person is being sought as part of the investigation, with several others not currently suspected of criminal offenses affected by it.

The stated date for the plot to attack Cologne's synagogue, late March this year, would have roughly coincided with a series of crimes in Europe targeting Jewish people or institutions in the weeks after the outbreak of war with Iran.

These included an explosion in front of Liege synagogue in Belgium on March 9, which caused property damage but no injuries.

Police in the Netherlands investigated a fire at Rotterdam's synagogue a few days later. An explosive device was set off outside a Jewish school in Amsterdam soon after, prompting heightened security across the Netherlands.

In London, a Jewish ambulance service was targeted in arson attacks in March, not long before two Jewish men were stabbed in broad daylight in what investigators treated as a likely act of terrorism.

Several months later, in September, police in Wuppertal in Germany arrested an Afghan national on suspicion of trying to set a fire at the city's synagogue.

#273. AI is straining America’s open records systems

Startups are mining public data for AI products, while citizens use chatbots to file more requests.

In Panton, Vermont, population 660, town clerk Kyle Rowe did it all. He crafted budgets, paid vendors, handled property tax disputes, and served as the town’s zoning supervisor and presiding elections officer. During morning office hours at the town hall—a wood-frame structure built as a church in 1858—he also fielded public records requests. Recently, he got rather busy.

Panton used to get a request every year or so from a company called SmartProcure for “all purchasing records,” covering everything from road salt to computers to toilet paper. Last year, those requests started coming quarterly. Then different companies began making more specific requests, like records of every purchase related to emergency road flares. These targeted inquiries started coming monthly or more. “I’m happy to answer public records requests from people,” says Rowe, who recently moved into a position at a nearby town. “But answering it for these purposes—it feels like I’m doing unpaid opposition research on the taxpayers’ time.”

Rowe’s experiences are being repeated across the US. While data brokers have mined public records for decades, AI has intensified investors’ interest. Over the last few years, venture-backed startups have raised upwards of $100 million to collect data from thousands of agencies and turn it into AI-powered “signals” that help businesses sell to governments.

At the same time, AI tools have made it easier for individuals to draft public records requests. Many places have seen double-digit annual increases in recent years. While more activity is good for democracy, AI-drafted requests tend to be longer, and broader in scope—and the offices answering them haven’t always grown in head count or budget.

As agencies struggle to tell whether they’re dealing with a citizen, a chatbot, or a sales pipeline, some states are passing legislation that makes it easier to deny requests, possibly making public offices less transparent.

The US Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) of 1966 established citizens’ right to know what their government is doing, and by now every state has written its own version into law. Greater transparency has led to cleaner drinking water, lower taxes, and better schools. But the system is far from perfect: Many requests linger for months, the process is often frustratingly bureaucratic, and rules and guidelines vary by state, county, and even town.

This is why businesses, with the time and resources to navigate this labyrinth, have often dominated FOIA since its early days. Margaret Kwoka, a law professor at Ohio State University and a recent member of the FOIA Advisory Committee, documented the trend in her 2016 study “FOIA, Inc.”

Her analysis found that commercial requesters of all kinds—regulated companies, government contractors, information resellers—have accounted for 79% to 96% of public records requests at federal agencies like the Environmental Protection Agency and the Food and Drug Administration. What Kwoka once described as a cottage industry of small shops reselling public records has become a lucrative market for “much more sophisticated and integrated database products,” she says.

SmartProcure (which does business as GovSpend) pioneered the model 15 years ago, with a standardized approach for collecting government purchasing data. Its requests are “handled by real people with long-standing relationships,” says Trip Colden, GovSpend’s chief operating officer, and the company has preferential pricing for agencies.

The newer AI startups promise to make selling to government faster and fairer. Starbridge has raised $52 million, including a Series A led by Craft Ventures (the firm of David Sacks, the former White House AI and crypto czar), to build the equivalent of a “Bloomberg Terminal for public sector data,” a reference to the pricey data consoles that are a fixture on Wall Street trading desks. The company describes its mission as getting “the best technology into the hands of public leaders,” with public records as one input that helps match agencies with vendors.Pursuit, backed by investors including Bill Gurley and Jack Altman, has raised $25.5 million to help companies identify likely government buyers, drawing on board minutes, budgets, and what it calls “an industrial-scale FOIA operation.” CEO and cofounder Mike Vichich says Pursuit’s data will benefit the public, noting that many towns are seeing costs rise faster than revenues and “competition is what saves taxpayers money.”

While incumbents employ account teams to build a rapport with agencies, several clerks and county attorneys say newer startups often send many requests as they scramble to catch up on historical data. For example, PinPoint Analytics, which analyzes construction bid data, sent as many as 2,000 requests per day while building its dataset before settling closer to 500 today, says chief operating officer Mark Zurada. That mirrors the activity of SmartProcure and Pursuit, which send roughly 180,000 requests per year, according to their websites.

But the numbers can be much higher. NationGraph, which serves midsize vendors such as janitorial service providers, claims to send about 10,000 requests per day on behalf of clients; the company did not respond to requests for comment.The requests that companies send are typically written with templates, not AI. But AI helps standardize what comes back—spreadsheets, PDFs, mailed packets—and analyze it all to create branded sales “signals,” or benchmarks to help the business clients set their prices.

In small towns, this activity can be an annoyance; in cities and counties, which get many times the volume, handling it is becoming a full-time job. Chautauqua County, New York, hired a paralegal this summer after seeing requests double—an increase its county attorney blamed on people using ChatGPT to generate requests and on others seeking records to resell.

In Ann Arbor, Michigan, chief deputy clerk Sarah Alanis has seen the number of requests climb from 581 in 2021 to 937 last year—“our new normal is high,” she says. A growing share comes from requesters harvesting data at scale, sometimes asking for purchases from “vendors that don’t have much to do with one another,” or ones the city has never used. FOIA used to take a few hours of her week; now it’s often half her day, she told the Michigan Advance earlier this year.

It’s not just sales tech—AI tools have made it easy for anyone to fire off requests. Federal agencies received a record 1.7 million last year, which a New York Times report attributed partly to AI, as well as to mass filings by the Heritage Foundation and a rise in the number of immigrants seeking their own records for legal protection. David Cuillier, director of the Brechner Freedom of Information Project at the University of Florida, ran the US Department of Education’s July request log through an AI detector and concluded that at least 29% of requests had been written at least partly by AI, up from almost none before 2025. The AI-written requests were twice as long, and 83% asked for long lists of records.

In Pennsylvania, AI-driven activity is “breaking records every month,” says Liz Wagenseller, executive director of the Office of Open Records, which fields appeals for denied requests. Volumes had surged before—during the covid years, at the height of the 2020 election fight, or amid battles over school curricula. But Wagenseller says this wave isn’t driven by a hot-button issue, and appeals keep rising—from about 3,000 in 2021 and just under 4,000 in 2025 to a projected 6,000 this year.

While more activity signals stronger civic engagement, AI is straining an already fragile infrastructure with often poorly drafted requests. Wagenseller notes that when it comes to appealing a denial, chatbots “always give [people] encouragement to try,” even when it has no chance. Filings that used to take a paragraph now run pages. Some contain hallucinated legal citations, and one even included the user’s prompt to Claude.

On the other side of the records requests, resource-strapped offices are using tech to manage it all. One-fifth of federal agencies report using AI or machine learning to help search for records. The Washington Post reported that the Department of Homeland Security is using AI to speed redactions, which transparency advocates worry could lock in agencies’ long habit of withholding more than the law requires. Local governments are catching up, with many still migrating from email to centralized request portals. The software vendor CivicPlus says its NextRequest platform handles more than a million requests a year and uses captchas to screen out bots. That stops automated agents, says chief marketing officer Jane Snyder, but it “doesn’t determine whether a person used AI to help draft a request.”

As volumes rise, legislatures are responding. CivicPlus counts more than 20 state and federal measures in play this year, several of which give agencies new ways to say no. California’s, signed in September, declares that AI systems are not “members of the public,” though people may still use AI “at an ordinary human volume and frequency.” A stalled Pennsylvania bill would let agencies deny requests they “reasonably suspect” were generated by a script or AI. Wagenseller doesn’t think that’s the answer. The real choice, she says, is funding agencies to keep up or making the system less free, fast, and open—“and you’re giving up something for both.”

Arguably the most aggressive action yet has been in Indiana, where Allen County officials described a growing trend in “suspiciously non-human” requests for years of purchase orders, eating up to 20 hours a week of staff time, as reported by the Journal Gazette. A state law that passed without a single dissenting vote and took effect July 1 lets agencies charge out-of-state requesters, prioritize residents, and deny requests they suspect are aimed at data scraping or phishing.

Neighboring Adams County went further. In March, it banned commercial use of its records, including resale. The county still hands over the documents, though; a notice of the ban is attached, but there are few means to enforce it. Requests had jumped from about one a week to as many as 10, often in a single burst; since the state law took effect, they’ve settled at one to five. County attorney Clayton Lengerich says the new rules don’t affect “any individual requester’s ability to keep their local municipality accountable,” only requests that “someone’s going to throw into an AI generator for some sales analysis.”

Fielding FOIA requests is expensive, and someone has to pay. Congress tried to put the responsibility on business in 1986, amending FOIA to let agencies charge commercial requesters more, but the rules were so riddled with exceptions that this rarely happens. “It costs more for the agencies to collect the fees than it’s worth in fees, and so they just don’t,” says Kwoka, the Ohio State law professor. She estimates that agencies recoup less than 5% of their costs from commercial requesters; at the FDA in one year she studied, it was $328,000 against $33.6 million spent.

Kwoka has long argued for “affirmative disclosure,” or proactively posting the information that gets asked for most. She points to the EPA, which put property contamination records online after commercial buyers had requested them one address at a time for years. A handful of states have adopted portals, such as California’s Open FI$Cal, that regularly publish high-level spending data. But this doesn’t include the full contracts that sales-tech firms often request, which reveal expiration dates, termination clauses, and service commitments.

Startups like Pursuit and Starbridge say they’d welcome this approach, and they seem confident their business model could survive if the data became freely available. “The best request is one that no one has to file because the data is already out there,” says Vichich. But publishing isn’t free, and commercial requesters also aren’t raising their hands to fund the fix.

As states negotiate reforms, the biggest risk is that rules built to limit bulk AI requests or sales-tech crawlers will land on everyone else: out-of-state reporters, academic researchers, immigration lawyers. Meanwhile, the requests keep increasing. “It’s something we’re going to have to hold our nose and continue doing,” says Rowe, the small-town Vermont clerk. “The alternative sets a dangerous precedent for a person being able to hold government accountable.”

Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible.

An exclusive interview with Nick Cammarata, the researcher whose 26,000-word viral blog post has AI safety folks celebrating.

With the rise of personal AI assistants, the internet isn't just for humans anymore.

The startup Tau Robotics is sending humanoid robots to clean San Francisco homes. They still need lots of human guidance, but they’re learning.

#270. Germany news: Cologne court awards record damages in Catholic sex abuse case

A court has awarded the highest damages ever in Germany to a victim of sexual abuse linked to the Catholic Church. An alleged spy and suspected terrorists are also making headlines in Germany on Thursday.

Below is a roundup of the top news stories from Germany from Thursday, November 26, 2026:

Michael Noetzel, the new justice minister in the eastern state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, has come under fire for a now-deleted social media post promoting the far-left antifa.

The controversy centers on a photo of Noetzel wearing a T-shirt with the historic 1932 antifa logo and raising his left fist.

Noetzel, a representative of the socialist Left Party, also wrote that it is important for young people to attend antifa meetings.

Philipp Amthor, who serves as acting head of the state chapter of the conservative CDU, demanded that Noetzel "make an unambiguous statement now regarding his position on left-wing extremist and violence-prone groups within the antifa scene."

Enrico Schult, who is a parliamentary group leader of the far-right populist AfD, said: "If you have such a hard time distancing yourself from violent structures, then you are unfit to serve as minister of justice."

The ministry stated that Noetzel "naturally takes a clear stand against extremism."

The ministry also identified right-wing extremism as the greatest threat to democracy and that combating it is a priority.

The German government plans to acquire a stake in the Canada-based artificial intelligence technology firm Cohere for the symbolic sum of €1.

The Digital Ministry confirmed media reports that the Finance Ministry had approved the government's small stake in the multinational company.

According to a ministry spokesperson, the government is currently considering investing a larger sum.

Cohere would commit itself "to helping increase competitiveness in AI in Germany and to securing jobs, research and development and investment in Germany," the spokesperson said.

He added that the German government would receive "specific governance guarantees that safeguard the goal of digital sovereignty."

Cohere's goal is to develop sovereign AI services for the public administration, as well as finance, defense, energy, telecommunications, and healthcare.

This technology is designed to operate independently of major US data center operators.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The trial of a German-Ukrainian woman charged with spying for Russia began in Berlin.

The start of the proceedings was delayed in the morning after the accused developed health problems that required treatment by emergency medical workers, a spokeswoman for a Berlin court said.

Later, however, she was brought into the courtroom in a wheelchair, wearing dark sunglasses.

Several times throughout the afternoon, the defense attorneys said their client was feeling nauseous, and a bucket was brought in. A doctor was present in the courtroom.

The trial is expected to last until May 2027.

Read more about the charges against the woman, as well as the diplomatic fallout caused by the case.

IG Metall, representing millions of workers in Germany's metal and electrical industry, is the country's largest trade union.

The deal came after more than 24 hours of talks with employers.

Read the full story on what the union and industry leaders agreed to.

Germany national player Laura Freigang has been banned from playing until October 7, 2027, over three doping tests she missed, meaning that she will not be available to participate in the World Cup in Brazil next year, the German Football Federation (DFB) said in a statement on Thursday.

The ban comes amid a settlement between Freigang, 28, who is also the captain of Frankfurt Eintracht, and the DFB, the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) and Germany's National Anti-Doping Agency (NADA).

Freigang has been the subject of proceedings for several months, having been accused of not being at the location she specified for a doping control on three occasions between March 2025 and February 2026.

In June, she said that the missed tests "were not deliberately avoided appointments but inconsistencies or misunderstandings in the comprehensive details that have to be updated daily and which we as national team players have to update in the system on a daily and hourly basis."

Freigang has played 45 times for Germany, scoring 17 goals.

However, she has not recently been a regular in the team.

Read the full story on why Freigang will miss the 2027 World Cup.

The archdiocese in the western city of Cologne was ordered on Wednesday to pay a woman who was sexually abused by a priest for years €550,000 ($601,865) in damages — the highest amount a German court has ever awarded to a victim of abuse in theCatholic Church.

That amount will, however, by offset by the €360,000 that the Catholic Church's Independent Commission for Recognition Payments has already paid to the claimant.

The woman had previously had her claim rejected by the Cologne Regional Court, which, although it accepted that the victim had been severely sexually abused by a priest in the 1970s and 1980s, argued that the archdiocese could not be made responsible for the crimes because the man had acted "more or less as a private individual."

The higher regional court has now overturned that ruling at an appeal, saying that the priest had approached the claimant "under the cover of his church work" when he was a deacon.

It said he used his standing in the church to be allowed to take in foster children, of whom the claimant was one.

The priest was sentenced to 12 years in prison in 2022.

German Foreign MinisterJohann Wadephul has warned against an expansion of the Ukraine conflict into other regions after the Ukrainian attacks on Russian ships in Libya.

"Ukraine's ​right to self-defense is undisputed and we ​do support Ukraine, but I strongly ⁠warn ​against allowing ​this conflict to spread ​geographically," he ‌said at ​a ⁠press conference in Berlin with ⁠his ​Romanian counterpart Dan Neculaescu.

Wadephul also condemned reported Russian attacks on two foreign freight ships said to be carrying grain near Ukraine's Black Sea port of Odesa, saying such attacks did not concern only the security of nearby nations but also the food security of people in the Global South.

"It is clear that we cannot accept drone attacks on trading vessels," he said. "NATO will therefore step up its engagement in the region."

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier has called for closer economic and political partnerships with African countries as he wound up what was probably his last trip to the continent as head of state.

Speaking in Kenya, Steinmeier said that there were great variations in the state of development between individual countries and even within some of them.

"But I believe it is worthwhile investing in Africa and in relations with African countries," he said.

He said this was not just meant with a view to possible investment by German companies drawn by Africa's mostly young national populations and developing markets.   "That is true, but we should not limit our view to that. Many African countries now have political weight and growing self-confidence and want a say in shaping the future of the world," he said. "Africa, it has become clear, is a continent that requires patience if you want to discover it," Steinmeier said. "There is no single Africa, but very many."

Before Kenya, Steinmeier visited Ivory Coast and Ghana. On the final day of his trip, he went to the Crescent Island nature reserve on Lake Naivasha, an area under threat from climate change.

Chocolate manufacturers in Germany produced less in 2025 than the year before.

According to figures from the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis) released on Thursday, around 1 million metric tons (1.1 US tons) of chocolate products containing cocoa were made in Germany in 2025, compared with 1.1 million tons in 2024.

Much of the chocolate produced in Germany is exported (916,200 tons in 2025), while considerable amounts are also imported (530,000 tons in 2025), with a quarter of that amount coming from neighboring Belgium.

Altogether 13.4% of exports went to France, followed by Poland (9.6%) and the UK (9.3%).

According to Destatis, citing the EU's statistical agency Eurostat, Germany remains the European leader in the production of gingerbread, or Lebkuchen, manufacturing 39.4% of the entire EU supply of the sweet treat, compared with Poland on 17.3% and the Netherlands on 17%.

German authorities say that two Iraqi citizens believed to be members of a pro-Iranian terrorist group have been arrested on suspicion of having planned a number of anti-Jewish attacks, including on a synagogue in the western city of Cologne.

You can read more about the arrests and the charges laid against the two men in our article: Germany: 2 arrested, suspected of plotting synagogue attack

A survey by police union GdP has shown that some 69% of police in Germany are in favor of a ban on private fireworks on New Year's Eve.

According to the survey of 9,000 members, more than 70% feel that the situation for police on the evening would improve if such a ban were in place.

Altogether 54% of respondents who had been on duty during the past 10 years of New Year's Eve festivities reported having been in a dangerous or threatening situation caused by fireworks.

A whole 195 respondents said they had been injured by fireworks on the evening.

The poll was prompted by an open letter to Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt by a group calling itself #böllerciao (Goodbye firecrackers) with some 1.17 million signatories. The name is a play on the famous anti-Nazi song Bella Ciao.

The group includes 86 organizations, among them Environmental Action Germany (DUH) and the GdP, who have called for a ban on private fireworks to protect people, emergency personnel, animals and the environment.

Plans foreseeing a rise of €1 billion ($1.1 billion) in the budget for the Interior Ministry have been approved by the three parties in Germany's coalition government, after much debate centering on something that makes up a relatively small proportion of that money: the controversial planned centers for rejected asylum seekers in Rwanda.

According to Klaus-Peter Willsch of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU), just €5 million are earmarked for the so-called return hubs, shared between several European countries.

He said the €20 million that has often been cited as being for the Rwanda migration centers was not only for the hubs in that country, but for other potential projects in third countries as well.

Despite the relatively small amounts of money involved, the Rwanda plans devised by Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU) along with Austria, Denmark, the Netherlands and Greece came under fire not only from coalition partners the Social Democrats (SPD) but particularly from opposition parties.

The Green Party and the Left Party both rejected the idea for ethical reasons, with Green lawmaker Leon Eckert speaking of "state-organized human trafficking," while Dietmar Bartsch of the Left pointed out that the deal was being made with an authoritarian regime.

The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD), for its part, said it found the plans too soft, with parliamentarian Marcus Bühl calling them a "smoke screen," as just 20 rejected asylum-seekers from Germany were to be initially sent to Rwanda under the scheme.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Dobrindt defended the scheme, saying that the opposition was trying to stir up controversy about a concept that had been approved at European level. He also called criticism of the political system in Rwanda inappropriate, citing a school for Afghan girls that had been set up in the country amid the ban on secondary education for females by the Taliban government.

The interior minister also praised the additional funds given to his ministry as a contribution to Germany's defense against hybrid attacks from Russia, with a rise in the budgets of both the IT security and the civic protection departments.

The draft 2027 budget, which was approved by the conservative CDU/CSU bloc and the SPD, however includes less funding for the BAMF migration authority (from €999 million in 2026 to €994 million) and for integration aid for migrants and refugees (down €328 million to €1.07 billion).

The trial of a German-Ukrainian woman due to go on trial on Thursday on charges of spying for Russia was delayed in the morning after the accused developed health problems that required treatment by emergency medical workers, a spokeswoman for a Berlin court said.

It was not clear whether her trial could go ahead as planned.

The 57-year-old woman has been accused of passing information to an officer from Russia's GRU intelligence agency who was posing as a diplomat at the Russian Embassy in Berlin.

Prosecutors allege that she used contacts with  current and former German Defense Ministry officials to collect information on military aid for Ukraine, drone test sites and the arms industry.

She also faces accusation of having provided her alleged handler access to key political events in Berlin.

The Bundestag is conducting its concluding debates on the budget for 2027 ahead of a final vote scheduled for Friday.

On Thursday, the focus will initially be on the individual budget for the Interior Ministry led by Alexander Dobrindt of the conservative Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU), the sister party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU).

The government foresees that the ministry, which is responsible for the federal police and the domestic intelligence agency BfV, among other things, will receive some €16.8 billion in 2027 ($18.43 billion), around €1 billion more than this year.

Lawmakers will then go on to debate the individual budgets for the Economics and Energy Ministry, the Ministry for Housing, Urban Development and Building, the Ministry of Food and Agriculture and the Ministry for Education, Family Affairs, Senior Citizens, Women and Youth.

"We will no longer be able to afford everything with tax revenue that we have become all too accustomed to for far too long," Merz added.

#267. CEOs are tired of being held responsible for gun regulation

Americans have grown used to corporate executives treading the well-worn paths of the Northeast corridor to convene alongside elected officials in Washington, DC, and discuss geopolitics, policy and all that’s in-between.

In 2017, major CEOs from across the country came together to oppose North Carolina’s transgender bathroom law. In 2019, they called abortion bans “bad for business.”

After the deadly attack on the US Capitol on January 6, 2021, many of corporate America’s biggest names denounced the rioters and pledged to halt their political giving.

Recently, more than 1,000 companies promised to voluntarily curtail their operations in Russia in protest of Moscow’s war on Ukraine.

Dick’s Sporting Goods stopped selling semi-automatic, assault-style rifles at stores and Citigroup put new restrictions on gun sales by business customers after the mass shooting at a high school in Parkland, Florida, in 2018.

A year later, after mass shootings at a Walmart in El Paso, Texas, and a nightclub in Dayton, Ohio, Walmart ended handgun ammunition sales.

Corporate leadership has long been vocal on the issue of gun control – in 2019 and again this past summer nearly 150 major companies – including Lululemon, Lyft, Bain Capital, Bloomberg LP, Permanente Medical Group and Unilever – called gun violence a “public health crisis” and demanded that the US Senate pass legislation to address it.

That’s why corporate America’s silence in the wake of the latest mass shooting at a school in Nashville is so jarring. The United States has come to rely on the increasing power of large corporations as political advocates.

But Yale professor Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, a vocal advocate of corporate social responsibility who has a direct line to major CEOs around the globe, said that top executives are forlorn. Their previous efforts haven’t done much to push the needle on gun control legislation and without more backing, they don’t know what else they can do at the moment, he said.

Before the Bell spoke with Sonnenfeld, who runs Yale School of Management’s Chief Executive Leadership Institute, a nonprofit educational and research institute focused on CEO leadership and corporate governance.

This interview has been edited for clarity and length.

Before the Bell: CEOs have been quiet about gun reform since the latest mass school shooting in Nashville, have you heard anything about plans to speak out?

Jeffrey Sonnenfeld: Where is everybody else? Where is all of civil society? CEOs are just one group of people and it’s like we’re turning to them to be our saviors on every topic. They’ve joined causes with valor and nobility but they can’t just be taking cause after cause as if there’s nobody else in society. The social change that happened in the 1960s wasn’t being led primarily by CEOs. Social changes really happened when we saw the interfaith activity of clergy locking arms and canvassing legislators. We saw campuses alive and aroused. Where’s all the student activism?

The CEOs are still the most active even if they’re less active than they were six months ago. They’re not there as hired hands of shareholders to fill the role of politicians and civic leaders. They’re there to join that chorus, but they don’t want to be the only one singing.

So is this what you’re hearing from top CEOs? Have they gotten tired of advocating?

I just got off of a CEO call on voting rights and this morning we had a forum on sustainability – CEOs are still the most active on these fronts. It’s the same thing on immigration reform. If a CEO was working an 18 hour day on a 12 day week, they still couldn’t address all of the issues that need addressing.

The nation’s CEOs are waiting for everybody else to join them. They don’t need to restate something they’ve already stated. They’ve jumped in the pool, where’s everybody else?

So what do you think has led to this complacency amongst Americans and the growing reliance on CEOs to advocate on our behalf?

They’ve taken a very strong stance and they’ve gone out further than the general public. They are where the general public is on surveys, but they’re not where the general public is on action in the streets. So we’re ready for others to now do something. Enough already on saying ‘what are the CEOs doing?’ Social capital is as valuable as financial capital. CEOs understand that in their soul, they want there to be social capital. They want there to be public trust, but they need the rest of civil society to join them. And that’s their frustration.

But don’t these CEOs hold the purse strings in terms of donating to powerful politicians?

You would think that, but since the 2020 elections much less of campaign contributions have come from big business. Since the 2021 run on the Capitol, a lot of businesses either had an official moratorium or they’ve given mere pennies to politicians. The common impression on the street that CEOs are controlling campaign purses strings is 100% wrong.

Tesla reported. a modest 4% rise in sales in the first quarter compared to the final three months of last year, despite a series of price cuts on its lower priced vehicles and talk by CEO Elon Musk about strong demand at those lower prices.

The first quarter also marked the fourth straight quarter that Tesla has produced more vehicles than it has delivered to customers. Some of that may be due to the ramp up in production at two new factories, one in Texas, the other in Germany, which opened last spring, and a lag between that increased production and sales.

Tesla said there was an increase in the number of its more expensive models, the Model S and Model X, in transit to Europe, the Middle East and Africa, as well as to the Asia Pacific region.

But it does mean that over the last 12 months Tesla has produced 78,000 more cars than it has sold, suggesting that talk of strong demand by Tesla executives may not be backed up by the numbers.

“Early this year, we had a price adjustment. After that, we actually generated a huge demand, more than we can produce, really,” said Tom Zhu, Tesla’s executive in charge of global production and sales. “And as Elon said, as long as you offer a product with value at affordable price, you don’t have to worry about demand.”

#265. How data centers are driving a US natural-gas boom

Rising electricity demand is locking in fossil-fuel generation.

In May 2025, my colleague David Rotman wrote a feature story describing how AI could keep us dependent on natural gas. Just 18 months later, I’ve lost count of how many times he’s already been proved right.

Sure, it’s technically possible to meet the world’s rising electricity demand with other power sources, including renewables like wind and solar supported by batteries. But the reality in the US so far is that the data center boom is helping to fuel a massive natural-gas resurgence.

Just one example: Plans for the Meta data center in Louisiana that David focused on in his story have expanded, and its power needs have too. The local utility went from three planned natural-gas plants to 10. And as I wrote in a new story this week, data center developers are now looking beyond the grid and planning to build their own off-grid gas power plants. How did we get here?

If you want to understand the future of the grid, one way to do it is by looking at interconnection queues—lists of power plants that have requested a connection to the system. In recent years these queues have been dominated by renewables like wind and solar power, which are generally the cheapest way to build new energy capacity today.

But there’s been a shift in some places, particularly for PJM, the country’s largest power grid operator, which covers parts of 13 states in an area stretching from Illinois to Washington, DC. PJM has seen a major uptick in natural-gas proposals. In August, the operator announced that it had accepted proposals for 715 total projects with a capacity of over 200 gigawatts to join its queue. Nearly half that total capacity represented natural-gas plants.

If all the projects in the queue were built, it would increase the fossil-fuel share on PJM’s grid from 61% to 67%, according to an analysis by Kevin Kircher, an energy modeler and assistant professor of mechanical engineering at Purdue.

PJM’s queue is reflective of a bigger trend across the US. Natural gas is already the single biggest source of electricity in the country, and it has basically become the default to meet exploding power demand.

This AI-driven rush is already affecting greenhouse-gas emissions for tech companies. Meta’s emissions are up 45% over last year’s, according to the company’s recently released 2026 Sustainability Report. That’s even higher than the jumps from fellow hyperscalers Google (18%), Amazon (16%), and Microsoft (25%). The company is also “reevaluating” its 2030 goal to reach net-zero emissions, according to the report, though there aren’t details about how or when it might reach a decision there.

And there’s another tidbit in that Meta report worth noting: The company said that when the grid can’t deliver power “on the necessary timeline,” it will look to other methods, including building its own on-site power generation.

This fits into a related and growing trend that I’ve been tracking recently: Data center developers are looking to bypass long wait times to hook up to the grid by building their own power plants instead.

It’s not new for large industrial facilities to supply their own power. Chemical plants often have natural-gas infrastructure on-site to generate electricity and heat, for example (though they’re generally connected to the grid as well). Mining operations are often remote, requiring an off-grid power source.

But the desire to come online quickly means there could be a massive boom in off-grid power plants for data centers. Over 100 such facilities have been proposed in the US, with a total capacity of 115 gigawatts (that’s more than double the entire peak power demand of California). The vast majority of these sites have been proposed since the beginning of 2025.

There are alternative ways to help meet growing electricity demand: Wind and solar are inexpensive options, and pairing them with batteries could improve their reliability, for example. I’ve also written before about demand flexibility—efforts to limit power drawn from the grid when demand is high.

Right now, though, the evidence continues to stack up that the AI boom in the US is basically synonymous with a natural-gas boom.

#264. 2026’s Best Black Friday Deals: We’ve Been Tracking Since 4 AM

The Black Friday deals have arrived! Set yourself up with a turkey sandwich and a warm drink, because it's time to shop the best sale event of the year. And after the year we've had, we could all use a few bargains to cheer us up, score that upgrade we've been needing, and get a few gifts in the bag.

The Reviews team at WIRED tracks prices on our favorite gadgets year-round, and we highlight deals only on devices we’ve tested and would recommend to our own friends and family. These are the discounts that caught our eye—vetted for price hikes and fake deals. And if you’re looking for something more distinctive and gift-worthy, we’ve curated some special finds on sale.

Updated Friday, November 27, at 1:45 pm ET: We’ve added new gaming deals and our favorite deals under $100. We also updated prices and removed deals no longer available.

Additional contributors: Louryn Strampe, Scott Gilbertson, Nena Farrell, Kat Merck, Molly Higgins, Boutayna Chokrane, Luke Larsen, Harry Rabinowitz, Les Shu

Curated by Cooper Fleishman, executive commerce director. Updated Friday, November 27, at 2:30 pm ET.

The Dell XPS 13 was already a great deal, with its aggressive starting price and beautiful display. And then comes along this discount, which brings the price down to just $550. A laptop this premium for under $600 feels outrageous, even if it only comes with 8 GB of RAM and 256 GB of storage. If you’re using this for work or school, you might want to consider the upgraded 16-GB model, which is also on sale for Black Friday. There’s no laptop deal quite like it right now. —Luke Larsen

Gaming laptops have gotten really expensive over the past year—to the point where I could no longer recommend any of the available options around $1,000. This deal gets close though, bringing it down to its cheapest price ever. It’s almost unheard of to find a gaming laptop with an RTX 5060 at this price, especially since this also comes with a terabyte of storage. This is a chunky boy at almost an inch thick, but hey, that’s not uncommon for gaming laptops in this price range. —Luke Larsen

I don’t normally recommend two-year-old laptops. But this is the cheapest price the Surface Laptop has dropped to this entire year, making it worth buying again. Personally, I love the 3:2 aspect ratio, which gives it a taller form factor than standard laptops. And beyond that, it’s one of the most premium-feeling laptops you can buy on the Windows side. I should note that this one isn’t the latest version with the newer chips, but for $900, it’s still great. Just know that you’re only getting 256 GB of storage. —Luke Larsen

I’ve often called the MacBook Air the laptop most people should buy. Even after testing dozens of new laptops this year, I stand by that statement. It balances price, battery life, performance, and quality in a way that’s still unbeaten by the competition. The only problem is that at its retail price of $1,299, it’s been a bit too expensive. At a full $250 off, though, it’s a must-buy. —Luke Larsen

As Apple’s entry-level laptop, the MacBook Neo hasn’t seen much of a sale since it came out this spring. But finally, the MacBook Neo is down $50 to just $649. While its direct competitor, the XPS 13, is cheaper, the Neo is the cheapest way into the macOS ecosystem, even though you’ll have to live with only 8 GB of RAM. —Luke Larsen

The Mac Mini has recently become a surprise hot product, primarily thanks to the surge of interest in running AI models locally. The Mac Mini works quite well as an affordable, always-on AI box for your home, especially if you upgrade it to at least 32 GB of RAM. In terms of price, this has been the standard discount that Amazon has been offering for the past month or so, but that doesn’t mean it’s not still a strong value. —Luke Larsen

The Mac Studio is a monster, but as you can tell by the price, it’s solely for creative pros and AI enthusiasts. The most powerful M5 Ultra model isn’t on sale, but you can take $200 off the M5 Max model, which still comes with 36 GB of RAM. Whether you’re a video editor or wanting an at-home, all-powerful AI box for coding, the Mac Studio is an absolute champ. —Luke Larsen

The base iPad is the one we recommend most people buy when shopping for a tablet. This particular discount isn’t out of the ordinary, but it’s still a competitive price for what you get. This isn’t the iPad to get for work, but you don’t want to pay more just to take notes, play games, and leisurely scroll. If that’s primarily what you want an iPad for, this is the one you want. —Luke Larsen

This is the previous-gen iPad Mini, so it doesn’t have the OLED screen and faster performance of the newer model. But if you’re just looking for a simple small tablet for reading books and playing games, the newer model might be overkill anyways—especially given the price. —Luke Larsen

If you need an iPad that can double for work on the go, the iPad Air is the one to get. The discount here is fairly standard, though it’s still $100 off the retail price you’d pay when buying directly through Apple. Whether you opt for the 11-inch or 13-inch screen, make sure to pair it with a Magic Keyboard attachment for the full iPad experience. —Luke Larsen

This is a great price for AirPods Pro 3, our de facto wireless earbud of choice for anyone with an iPhone. They are stacked with some of the best automated noise-canceling and transparency modes you can get in wireless earbuds, plus other useful features like accurate heart rate tracking (so you can track workout data without a fitness tracker) and live translation. —Harry Rabinowitz

Look, we see this price often for AirPods Max 2 whenever there is a big sale event. But anything to lower their crazy $550 MSRP is noteworthy, considering how great (and popular) they are for Apple fans. They have some of the best noise-canceling and transparency modes around, plus a clear, detailed sound profile that puts wireless earbuds to shame. —Harry Rabinowitz

Topping my guide of the best mesh Wi-Fi systems, the Wi-Fi 7 Netgear Orbi 770 Series is perfect for most families. It’s a tri-band mesh (2.4-, 5-, and 6-GHz) offering simple setup, stable and speedy internet connectivity, and expansive coverage. The stylish tower design is unobtrusive, the internal antennas ensure your whole home gets online, and it delivers the benefits of Wi-Fi 7, including MLO (Multi-Link Operation) to enable Wi-Fi 7 devices to connect on multiple bands at once. —Simon Hill

For folks with an Eero mesh looking to boost that backyard Wi-Fi, the Eero Outdoor 7 is a weatherproof dual-band Wi-Fi 7 router that extends coverage into your garden. Buy a pair, and you can set up a point-to-point connection to deliver up to hundreds of megabits per second, up to a half-mile away. Ideal if you need Wi-Fi in a distant barn, garage, or other outbuilding, or at the bottom of a big yard. This is the lowest price I’ve seen for this. —Simon Hill

This router will cover most homes and apartments up to around 2,000 square feet, with fast and reliable connectivity, and tops our best Wi-Fi routers guide. It’s only dual-band, so you miss out on the 6-GHz band, but you get all the other advantages of Wi-Fi 7. It also has a generous array of ports and comes with free security software and parental controls. Support for VPN service, separate IoT or guest networks, and AiMesh rounds out an excellent device. —Simon Hill

Standing desks are often quite expensive, which is to be expected. But this is one of the few affordable standing desks worth buying. It comes in a number of different sizes, colors, and styles, and the laminated top protects against spills. It’s not the simplest to set up, but as our testers have verified, the FlexiSpot EN1 makes up for it by being such an affordable upgrade to your home office ergonomics. —Luke Larsen

Keychron is our favorite brand of keyboards, but they tend to be expensive. This is the best option in the lineup that’s actually quite affordable. Despite being cheaper, it still has a lot of the hallmarks of Keychron’s keyboards, including the hot-swappable switches, retro design, and high-end build quality. —Luke Larsen

There’s no mouse as beloved as Logitech’s MX Master line, primarily known for its comfortable grip, customization, and quality. The latest model makes a number of small tweaks to improve the mouse even further, including intuitive gesture controls and haptic feedback. If you take your work seriously, the MX Master 4 will be an excellent inclusion in your home office setup. —Luke Larsen

I’m still astounded that you can buy a high-quality 4K monitor for such little money these days. The Dell 27 Plus is my top pick as the monitor most people should buy, and the fact that it’s nearly $200 only bolsters that recommendation even more. The only compromise is that it’s a bit limited in terms of ports, but you can upgrade to the S2725DC with USB ports. —Luke Larsen

If you want an office chair that’s truly premium, the Steelcase Gesture is our recommendation. It’s a comfortable, attractive chair that comes in multiple colors, and you’ll find different sale prices for those different colors if you have a preference. It looks elegant, has a nice cushy seat, and you can adjust the lumbar support with the built-in tabs. —Nena Farrell

We’ve liked a few different Staples chairs over the years for a great office chair under $200, and while the Staples Dexley is our current pick (currently on sale too, but only $10 off), the Staples Hyken has a better deal. It’s down to $128, and it’s a good pick over the Dexley if you’re shorter. These seats both have great airflow and include a headrest. —Nena Farrell

Don’t rely solely on cloud storage. For sensitive documents, photos, and other files, keep them private by storing them on a NAS server at home. WIRED reviewer Simon Hill guides you through setting one up, starting with the NAS DH4300 Plus. He found it easy to install, and you can access it remotely if it’s connected to the internet. It has four bays, so you can put in four SSDs (up to 128 TB). It also works great for backing up your computers. —Les Shu

Created from fabric scraps that would otherwise end up in a landfill, this thoughtfully constructed bag looks great and can carry everything you need for a weeklong trip. The pack straps and adjustable waist belt all tuck away neatly when you don't need them, turning this Allpa into more of a soft suitcase. —Scott Gilbertson

The Coraza is a gorgeous suitcase, and thanks to Cotopaxi's emphasis on ethical business, it's our top pick for the most sustainable carry on. Latched hard-shell luggage like the Coraza offers many of the benefits of an aluminum roller, but without the weight or the cost. If you want to upgrade your luggage without breaking the bank, the Coraza is a great choice. —Scott Gilbertson

Cotopaxi’s trim, colorful little bag swallows those odds and ends that would otherwise be careening around lose in your larger bag. It’s made from light recycled deadstock nylon and weighs in at a modest 6.5 ounces. The recycled fabric means your bag will be unique and the 4-liter capacity spread over three different compartments, gives you some organizational options. —Scott Gilbertson

Everything at Away Luggage is 25 percent off right now, including the Softside Carry-On, our top pick among roller bags. Multiple WIRED staffers own the hard-sided carry-on (currently $206 ($69 off) because it's good-looking and reasonably priced. However, former senior commerce editor Adrienne So prefers the brand's Softside Carry-On because it shows scuffs less easily, won't crack, and is more flexible if you overpack. —Scott Gilbertson

The Everywhere Tote is our favorite travel tote. Made from water-resistant nylon and accented with leather trim, I take the Everywhere Tote everywhere. It's the handbag you reach for when you're commuting, planning an overnight stay, or catching a flight. —Boutayna Chokrane

Gear editor Julian Chokkattu tests dozens of camera bags, and this roll-top model is his all-time favorite. Wandrd's popular Prvke (pronounced "provoke") now has zippered access to the rolltop, a larger side-access opening, and more internal organization. It's plenty roomy and well-sealed against the elements to protect your camera gear. —Scott Gilbertson

The Sony XM4C are finally on sale, and all is right in the world. These are essentially a version two of the cult-classic Sony WH-1000XM4, one of our favorite headphones of 2020, and one of Sony’s best-selling headphones ever. They are really the people’s choice: excellent sound, great noise-canceling (though not as good as Bose’s), a comfortable fit, a folding design, on-ear detection, and decent battery life, all at a reasonable price. —Harry Rabinowitz

With these and the Sony XM4C both at $200 for Black Friday, we’re spoiled for choice. In my review of the Bose QuietComfort Headphones (2nd Gen), my main gripe was price—these are great headphones that float in a strange price point between midrange and premium. That concern flies out the window with this excellent discount. They are supremely comfortable and have some of the best noise-canceling on the market—unmatched at this deal price of $200. —Harry Rabinowitz

The lowest price to date on my favorite pair of wireless earbuds? Sign me up. I lauded the Soundcore Liberty 5 Pro in my review because they punch way above their price point, giving much pricier earbuds a run for their money. But it’s call quality that blew me away: I sound better on these earbuds than any other I’ve tested, by far. —Harry Rabinowitz

Finally, a good sale on the Sony WH-1000XM6. This is the lowest price ever for arguably the best noise-canceling headphones you can buy. They go toe-to-toe with Bose for the best noise-canceling around, have a folding, travel-friendly design, and sound absolutely stellar. They set the bar for over-ear headphones, and remain one of the pairs I test others against when writing reviews. —Harry Rabinowitz

Our former top pick for best open earbuds, this pair was replaced only by its successor, the AeroClip 2. It’s also at its lowest price ever (by a lot). These open earbuds wrap around your outer ear, leaving your inner ear open to hear the world around you. They’re comfortable, water- and dust-resistant, and have excellent battery life, meaning you can wear them for outdoor exercise; a rainy dog walk; or anything, really. —Harry Rabinowitz

These are the best ANC earbuds, full stop. They have the strongest automated noise-canceling of any earbuds I’ve tested—New York City streets and busy cafes became a dim hum with ANC on. They also sound great, with clear, detailed instrumentation on some of my favorite albums. —Harry Rabinowitz

Art TVs act as decent televisions plus convincingly realistic wall art, and Samsung’s The Frame is the leader in the category. Do note that Samsung only offers 30 free art images—you'll need a $5 monthly subscription to the Samsung Art Store to access the full catalog of over 5,000. —Harry Rabinowitz

One of the best budget TVs at its lowest price ever. Really, getting picture quality that’s this good for under $1,000 is just silly. The TCL QM7L is bright, colorful, and detailed, according to WIRED contributor Rick Broida. Even the built-in speakers ain’t half-bad (though we still recommend getting a soundbar). —Harry Rabinowitz

Another great budget TV at its lowest price ever for Black Friday. Former WIRED reviewer Ryan Waniata highlighted the Hisense U7SG’s very high brightness and clear picture quality, especially for its price point. It comes in two versions: one with Google TV built in and one with Fire TV. (We prefer [and linked to] the Google TV model.) —Harry Rabinowitz

The Roku Pro Series OLED is our favorite budget OLED TV, on sale for the first time ever this Black Friday. It’s one of the lowest-priced OLEDs you can get, and comes with Roku’s easy-to-use operating system (and remote), so it’s a great option for non-techy people looking to try out an OLED screen. The main downside here is that it isn’t as bright as other non-OLED (or pricier OLED) options. —Harry Rabinowitz

Here’s the thing: Like many consumer tech companies, Roku raised prices significantly across its product lines. The Black Friday sale price for the Streaming Stick Plus With Voice Remote—our favorite streaming device for most people—was the same as the previous regular price. You once could have gotten this device for $20. Still, it’s a simple yet fantastic way to access streaming content on your TV, with support for tons of apps and easy navigation. And the current sale price makes it more palatable than the new MSRP. —Les Shu

While it’s a bit long, it’s not very tall, so it’s easy to fit in front of most TVs without blocking them. —Harry Rabinowitz

I used this soundbar for years. It’s one of the best compact, not-too-expensive models you can get. And it’s at its lowest price ever for Black Friday, likely spurred on by the release of the new (not on sale) Sonos Beam Ultra. The Gen 2 (along with the Bose TV Speaker [2nd Gen]) is the soundbar I recommend to people who are tight on space and just want something that works. —Harry Rabinowitz

This soundbar plus subwoofer is a fantastic way to upgrade your TV audio system for a reasonable price, especially with this discount. This tiny portable Bluetooth speaker is the smallest Sonos makes, but it has a leg up on the competition because it can still connect over Wi-Fi or Bluetooth. One of our favorite cordless vacuums, the V15 Detect is an oldie but a goodie. It's a great Dyson vacuum that was our top pick for a long time because it's more affordable than the Gen5Detect and V16, but still comes with two cleaner heads (the Digital Motorbar for carpet and Fluffy Optic for hard floors) and has 240 air-watts of suction (almost 100 more than the V10 Konical and other cheaper Dyson vacuums). —Nena Farrell

If you want the cheapest option for a robot vacuum while still getting good quality and mopping, Eufy’s Omni C28 did a great job cleaning multiple floors in my home, making it my overall favorite affordable vacuum pick to this day. For such a well-priced vacuum, it never got lost while navigating my home (a more expensive Eufy vacuum actually did get lost on me, funny enough) and can learn multiple maps if you need to clean more than one floor. It’s often on sale in the $400 range, so this price is the best I’ve seen. —Nena Farrell

If you’re looking for a new cordless vacuum but want to spend as little as possible (without buying garbage), you’re in luck: Our favorite affordable stick vacuum, the Bissell PowerClean, is on sale, making it even cheaper. It’s a great vacuum that stands upright, has HEPA filtration, and has four lights on the head to help illuminate dust and debris. You’ll get a crevice tool, a small upholstery tool, and a wall mount. —Nena Farrell

The Roborock Qrevo 2 Pro is one of my favorite affordable robot vacuums, especially when it’s on sale, and this is the lowest price you’ll find it for. Roborock’s vacuums have fantastic navigation and an easy-to-use app, and overall do a great job cleaning. The Qrevo 2 Pro especially impressed me with its extendable mop arm, which helps it get under cabinets and clean corners around the house. —Nena Farrell

This is the automatic litter box I recommend for anyone who wants a super-cheap, self-cleaning option without extra luxe features like a connected app or built-in camera. It has a familiar open-top design that most cats take to easily, and you control its functions with three buttons on the box: clean, refill litter, and power on/off. If you don’t want to break the bank but want to spend less time scooping urine and stool, I recommend this budget model. —Molly Higgins

This automatic litter box has an open, front-facing entrance and sits slightly raised on legs. It connects to Wi-Fi, so you can review your cat’s visits in the phone app. Each entry shows the time, your cat’s weight, and how long the visit lasted. During testing, it was easy to assemble and worked well—we think it’s worth considering, especially at a discount. —Molly Higgins

This pet water fountain is perfect for cats who love drinking from faucets. It features all-stainless-steel construction, which makes it more hygienic and keeps water colder. The tall spigot is great for cats who love long streams of water, and activated carbon filters sit below the steel top. Plus, the top has a reservoir, so water is always available. It's not app-connected, but the small window lets you easily monitor water levels. —Molly Higgins

Every cat parent should invest in an automatic pet water fountain. The flowing water encourages cats to drink, and staying hydrated can help your fur baby avoid potential health issues. We especially like this elegant glass fountain because glass harbors fewer bacteria than porous plastic. If you’re looking for a way to keep your pet’s water cleaner and fresher for longer, this could be just the solution. —Molly Higgins

This pet fountain has an intuitive, easy-to-use app that lets you monitor your pet's water intake, the fountain’s water level, and battery life. You can also set reminders for cleaning and filter replacements. The fountain has a wireless pump with a detachable basin that’s easy to remove and clean. It holds up to three liters of water and supports both 2.4-GHz and 5-GHz Wi-Fi for app compatibility. You can keep it plugged into the dock for a continuous flow, or move it around the house unplugged for up to 28 days on intermittent flow. —Molly Higgins

The Kindle Paperwhite is the best of Amazon’s e-readers to buy thanks to its larger screen and warm front light, plus 16 GB of storage. Don’t worry—you aren’t missing out on much; I recommend buying the on-sale model over the newest one, since the 12th gen is only two years old and still great. —Nena Farrell

This isn’t the best price I’ve seen the 2024 Kindle go for; even after the price hike this summer, I still saw it go on sale for $104 during Prime Day, which is a better discount than it has right now. But it’s still the cheapest Kindle you can shop so far during Black Friday. The base Kindle from 2024 is a good e-reader with a 6-inch screen, snappy performance, and access to the same Kindle system and software experience you’d get on more expensive models. —Nena Farrell

So far, this is my favorite deal you can find on a Kindle. I love using a Kindle Scribe as both an e-reader and a digital notebook, especially since it has a nice long battery life and easy-to-use software. I usually recommend the older, second-gen model since it’s cheaper and has most of the same features, but the third-gen Kindle Scribe is now on sale for less than the older one, so it makes sense to upgrade and pay less. My kind of Black Friday deal. —Nena Farrell

If you want the best e-reader that isn’t a Kindle (and the best-priced colorful e-reader, Kindle or not), the answer is a Kobo, specifically the Kobo Libra Colour. This e-reader has a 7-inch screen, built-in page-turn buttons, and a warm front light, and can be paired with the Kobo stylus so that it doubles as a digital notebook. It had a price hike earlier this year, raising it from $230 to $260, so this price isn’t a great deal compared to what it used to cost, but it’s better to buy it now than pay the new, higher price. —Nena Farrell

If you want the best digital notebook with all the bells and whistles, the ReMarkable Paper Pro is ReMarkable’s colorful and most powerful digital notebook yet. It offers one of the best writing experiences if you want a digital notebook that really feels like writing on paper, with a color screen and a gentle front light. Better yet, the bundle on sale will include the Marker Plus with an eraser and a protective folio. ReMarkable’s devices are rarely on sale, so don’t wait on this deal. —Nena Farrell

If you want a tablet focused on taking notes but not necessarily a digital notebook with an e-paper screen, the TCL Note A1 Nxtpaper is what you’re looking for. It gives you most of what we like about digital notebook devices, with software focused on note-taking, but it still works as an Android tablet so you can stream videos and use it like a regular tablet. —Nena Farrell

Three hundred dollars is an absolute steal for a top-performing blender you will likely only have to buy once in your life. —Kat Merck

I don’t love that this device markets itself as a “composter” when it really just grinds and dries your food scraps, but it’s the best one I’ve found under $300. #263. Crew member dies after diesel tanker sinks off Ibiza coast

Authorities rescued 17 crew members but one later died in hospital after a diesel tanker capsized off the Spanish island of Ibiza. A contingency plan against possible pollution damage is now in place.

A tanker carrying up to 7,000 metric tonnes (7,716 short tons) of diesel capzized off the Spanish island of Ibiza, local authorities said on Thursday.

The ship's 17 crew members were rescued but one later died in hospital and another six suffered from hypothermia when the Maltese-flagged Med Emre capsized overnight, the government of Spain's Balearic Islands, said in a statement.

According to emergency services, the five further crew members were taken to Valencia and the remainig five were in good condition on a ‌rescue ​vessel.

The chemical tanker was sailing from Algeciras to Barcelona when it capsized about 30 nautical miles (56 kilometers) off Ibiza's northwestern coast.

According to Spanish authorities, the Med Emre was drifting upside down northwest of Ibiza after capsizing. Initially, they said the ship had sunk to the seabed in 1,000 metres of water, but later corrected this statement.

The nationalities of the crew or the cause of the incident was not immediately clear.

The Transport Ministry said the maritime rescue vessel Guardamar Talia had reported no wreckage, floating debris or signs of pollution at the site as of Thursday morning. It added that another rescue ship was heading to the area to continue monitoring the situation.

Spain's maritime rescue service deployed an aircraft and the Clara Campoamor, a vessel equipped to respond to oil spills, to inspect the area.

Spain's merchant marine authority ​has activated the national maritime pollution contingency plan at level 2, the second-highest.

The Balearic regional government said it was assessing the incident and its potential impact, including the risk of fuel pollution, before deciding on further measures.

The waters surrounding Ibiza are a critical zone for biodiversity as they host sea turtles, dolphins and the ‌Balearic shearwater, one of Europe's most threatened seabirds.

The area also hosts vast Posidonia oceanica seagrass meadows, which are essential for maintaining marine biodiversity.

Emilio Rodriguez Diaz, a maritime security expert at the University of Cadiz, told Cadena SER radio that the area affected was "particularly vulnerable."

But he said the Med Emre was a modern ship, built in Turkey in 2019, with a double hull to ensure that, "in the event of a leak (or) a collision, that intermediate part between the cargo hold and the outer layer would flood."

"It's a kind of buffer that prevents the cargo... from being released into the environment," he said.

Spain's worst maritime environmental disaster happened in 2022, when the tanker Prestige sank off the northwestern Galicia region. It spilled tens of thousands of heavy fuel oil and polluted beaches across Spain and France.
